components.name: Parmesan
components.explain:
On an American menu, Parmesan is a generic word. In the United States Parmesan is defined by a federal standard of identity, a granular grating cheese cured at least ten months, wherever it is made. In the European Union it is the other way round: since a 2008 ruling of the European Court of Justice, only Parmigiano Reggiano may be sold as parmesan.

Parmigiano Reggiano is made only around Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena, with no preservatives, and is inspected at twelve months.

The Eggs Sardou prints Parmesan creamed spinach. The kitchen may use Parmigiano Reggiano, the Grana Padano already on the Caesar, or a domestic Parmesan; until the chef says which, call it Parmesan and nothing grander.

card.front: Does Parmesan on the Eggs Sardou mean Parmigiano Reggiano?
card.back: Not necessarily: in the US Parmesan is a generic name for a hard grating cheese, wherever it is made. Ask the kitchen which cheese goes into the creamed spinach.

producer.who: Parmesan, cheese and maker not printed
producer.where: As sourced: Parmigiano Reggiano is from Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena; American Parmesan may come from anywhere
producer.history:
The word Parmesan means different things on either side of the Atlantic. In the European Union, a 2008 ruling of the European Court of Justice held that only Parmigiano Reggiano, the protected cheese of Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena and parts of Mantua and Bologna, may be sold as parmesan. Its rules are strict: cows fed on fresh fodder and hay, no silage, no preservatives, dairies that make nothing else, and inspection at twelve months.

In the United States, Parmesan is a generic name. The federal standard of identity describes a granular cheese with a hard, brittle rind that grates readily, at most 32 per cent moisture and cured at least ten months; it says nothing about where the cheese is made.

So when an American menu prints Parmesan, as Brennan's does in the creamed spinach of the Eggs Sardou, it promises a hard grating cheese, not a particular one. The kitchen may use Parmigiano Reggiano, the Grana Padano it buys for the Caesar and the Shells & Cheese, which has its own card, or a domestic Parmesan. A server should know the difference and find out which.
facts: A 2008 European Court of Justice ruling reserves the name parmesan in the EU for Parmigiano Reggiano.

Parmigiano Reggiano is made around Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena and inspected at twelve months.
Parmigiano Reggiano allows no preservatives and no silage in the cows' feed.
notes: Say Parmesan creamed spinach, as printed; never upgrade it to Parmigiano Reggiano unless the kitchen confirms it.

producer.where: Arkansas City, Kansas (founded in Campbellsburg, Kentucky)
producer.history:
Creekstone Farms began in 1995, when John and Carol Stewart set up a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky. Stewart was a cattle geneticist at heart: he developed his own Angus line, sold bulls, genetics and semen to ranchers, and at one point owned the highest-marbling bull in the breed.

In 2003 the company moved into processing, buying a processing plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, where it began processing its own Premium Black Angus cattle in May 2003. Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to the low-stress handling standards of Dr. Temple Grandin. After BSE was found in the US herd in December 2003, Creekstone asked in 2004 to test every animal it slaughtered, and when the USDA refused, it took the question to court.

Stewart announced his retirement in October 2006. Sun Capital Partners had owned the business since 2005, and in 2017 it sold Creekstone to the Japanese trading house Marubeni Corporation, which owns it today. The company still buys its cattle on verifiable Black Angus genetics rather than hide colour, and its Natural Black Angus line carries the Certified Humane label.

At Brennan's the name is printed on three plates: both hanger steaks and the tenderloin of the Roasted Chateaubriand.

producer.history:
Vital Farms began in 2007, when Matt O'Hayer started with 20 hens on a 27-acre farm near Austin, Texas. The idea was eggs from hens that genuinely live outdoors, and the company built its standard around pasture: each hen has at least 108 square feet of rotated pasture, where it forages for grasses, succulents and wildflowers. That is the same figure the Certified Humane pasture standard sets, and the eggs carry that certification.

Rather than keep one great company flock, Vital Farms works with a network of small family farms, now numbering in the hundreds. In 2017 it opened its own egg washing and packing plant in Springfield, Missouri, which it calls Egg Central Station, and a second Egg Central Station is being built in Seymour, Indiana.

The company went public on Nasdaq as VITL in July 2020 and is a Certified B Corporation. It sells butter as well as eggs.

On our menu the name appears once: the sunny-side-up egg on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, where the runny yolk meets the béarnaise.

producer.where: Raised in New York's Catskills; D'Artagnan is based in Union, New Jersey
producer.history:
The Rohan is D'Artagnan's own duck. D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison, who met working at a charcuterie shop in New York City. A farmer had the first domestically raised foie gras in the United States and needed someone to sell it, so the two started a company to do it, selling whole raw lobes to New York chefs. Daguin was born in Auch, in Gascony, the eldest child of the Michelin-starred chef André Daguin, and the company is named for the Gascon musketeer. It is based in Union, New Jersey.

D'Artagnan's blog introduced the Rohan in January 2012. It is a proprietary cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, bred to approximate a style of duck found in Normandy and named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan in Brittany. The birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills, cage-free and never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids, to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck. Daguin says the extra time deepens the flavour and improves the meat-to-bone ratio.

The result is rosy, tender, mild meat with a rich, buttery depth. Brennan's prints Rohan on the duck breast of the dinner tasting and on the confit leg of the Duck Confit Waffle.

producer.history:
The Nueske story starts with Wilhelm and Wilhelmina Nueske, who emigrated from Prussia to Wisconsin in 1887 and brought their family recipes and their way of smoking over applewood. Two generations later, in 1933, Robert Carl Nueske, known as R.C., then 19, left his grandparents, parents, two brothers and a sister to work the family farm at Wittenberg, traded his plough for a delivery truck, and sold the family's smoked bacon, hams and sausages to the resorts of northern Wisconsin.

In the 1940s he bought a butcher shop and designed and built six smokehouses. The method has barely changed since: the bacon is smoked for about a full day over embers of real Wisconsin applewood logs, which gives a sweet, rounded smoke.

The company is still family owned and run, now in its third generation, with Tanya Nueske as chief executive; she says the family smokes the way her grandfather did. Besides bacon it smokes hams, poultry and sausages.

At Brennan's the name is printed on one dish, the dinner Succotash, where the smoky bacon meets the sweet glazed summer vegetables.

The Succotash has bacon in it, so mention it when a guest orders vegetables expecting no meat; any dietary question goes to the kitchen.

producer.who: Grana Padano DOP, Consorzio di Tutela
producer.history:
Grana Padano traces itself to 1135 and the Abbey of Chiaravalle, a few kilometres south of Milan. Bernard of Clairvaux had chosen to reclaim the marshland there, and his Cistercian monks drained and farmed it. With more milk than they could drink, they made a hard cheese that kept, which they called caseus vetus, old cheese. Ordinary people named it for its texture instead: grana, grainy, and Padano, from the Po Valley.

The Consorzio di Tutela, which protects the name, was founded on 18 June 1954, uniting producers, refiners and merchants, and the European Union made Grana Padano a DOP in 1996. Every wheel, 24 to 40 kg, ages at least nine months; at nine months inspectors test it with a hammer, a needle and a probe, and only a wheel that passes is fire-branded. Some age beyond 24 months.

It is now the world's best-selling protected cheese, over 5.2 million wheels in 2022. Its rules are its own: it may be made in 32 provinces across five northern regions, the cows may eat silage, and lysozyme, a protein from egg white, may be used as a preservative. With its nine-month minimum it is a younger, milder and different cheese from Parmigiano Reggiano, not a lesser copy of it.

producer.sayIt: Grana Padano, the Po Valley's protected hard cheese, first made by Cistercian monks near Milan in 1135: nutty, grainy and a touch milder than Parmigiano.

producer.history:
Mimolette is the French answer to Dutch Edam. The story told in France is that Louis XIV, under the mercantilist policies of his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, wanted a native cheese to replace the Edam the French were buying. Another telling has Colbert's embargo on foreign goods leaving the people of Flanders without their favourite Dutch-style cheese, so they made it themselves. Either way, it was made around Lille, and to tell it apart from Edam it was coloured, first with carrot juice and later with annatto, the seed that gives its blazing orange.

As it ages, cheese mites, which the French call little affineurs, are allowed onto the rind. They eat into the crust, leaving the grey, pitted, moon-like surface, and help the cheese ripen. In 2013 the American FDA detained about a ton of Mimolette because the mites exceeded six per cubic inch; the restriction was lifted in 2014.

Today a large maker is the Normandy cooperative Isigny Sainte-Mère, which began making Mimolette, also called Boule de Lille, in 1951 with master cheesemakers recruited from the north, and sells it from young to extra-mature at 24 months.
facts: Traditionally made around Lille, said to be created under Colbert's policies to replace Dutch Edam.

notes: Say mee-mo-LET: the orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and butterscotch-sweet as it ages.
The mite story delights some tables and puts others off; offer it only to the curious.
No maker or age is printed; never say Isigny Sainte-Mère or a particular age unless the kitchen confirms it.
The orange is annatto, a plant colouring, the same seed that turns some cheddar orange; dietary questions about the colouring go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Mimolette, mee-mo-LET, the orange cheese of Lille, made in the seventeenth century to rival Dutch Edam, melted with Abita Amber.

producer.where: Alicante, Spain, and the Mediterranean coast from southern Catalonia to Valencia
producer.history:
The Marcona is a Spanish almond variety native to the province of Alicante, and grown along the Mediterranean coast in southern Catalonia, Castellón and Valencia. It is called the queen of almonds. It is shorter, wider and rounder than the long almonds of commercial orchards, softer and sweeter, and it has almost none of the bitter edge an ordinary almond carries.

Its oldest work is in sweets. Marcona is the almond of turrón, the nougat of Alicante and Jijona, made in Jijona since at least the sixteenth century, and of marzipan. Jijona grinds the almond to a fine paste for its soft turrón; Alicante uses it whole and toasted in the hard one.

At the table, Marcona is the tapas almond: blanched to slip off the skin, roasted or fried in olive oil, and dusted with salt, so it eats rich and tender with a gentle crunch, and sits well beside Sherry and cheese.

At Brennan's it appears twice: in the gremolata on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and in the banana leaf of the Gulf Fish en Papillote, with olives, sorghum and crab.
facts: Marcona is a Spanish almond variety native to the province of Alicante.
It is shorter, wider and rounder than standard almonds, with almost no bitterness.
It is the traditional almond of turrón; Jijona turrón is recorded from at least the sixteenth century.
Jijona turrón grinds it to a paste; Alicante turrón uses it whole and toasted.
It is usually served blanched, roasted or fried in olive oil, and salted.

producer.sayIt: Marcona almonds, the round, sweet almond of Alicante in Spain, buttery and tender, the one Spain eats with Sherry.

producer.who: Nocellara del Belice olives, Castelvetrano style
producer.history:
What Americans call a Castelvetrano olive is, strictly, a way of preparing an olive. The variety is Nocellara del Belice, grown in the Valle del Belice in south-western Sicily, a dual-purpose olive pressed for oil and cured for the table. One of its table preparations is named for the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley, and olives treated that way are sold in the United States as Castelvetrano olives.

The method explains the taste. The olives are picked young and green and washed in a lye and water solution, which strips their natural bitterness completely in a matter of weeks; they are then kept in brine without fermenting. Skipping fermentation keeps the vivid emerald colour and leaves a mild, buttery, almost sweet olive with a crisp bite. The Sevillian method, by contrast, debitters partly and ferments, for a sharper olive.

In 1998 Nocellara del Belice was awarded a Protected Designation of Origin, and the variety now carries two: Nocellara del Belice DOP table olives and Valle del Belìce DOP extra virgin olive oil, which must be at least 70 per cent Nocellara.

Castelvetrano names a preparation, after the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley.

producer.where: Torreglia, near Padua, Italy (founded in Zara, Dalmatia)
producer.history:
In 1817 Girolamo Luxardo moved to Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, as consular representative of the Kingdom of Sardinia. His wife, Maria Canevari, made rosolio maraschino at home, a cherry liqueur of the region, and in 1821 he founded a distillery to make it properly. Within eight years the Emperor recognised it as superior. Around 1905 the plant at Zara made the first Luxardo maraschino cherries, marasca cherries candied in their own syrup, and in 1913 Michelangelo Luxardo, the third generation, built a new distillery.

The war ended all of it. Allied bombing from November 1943 to October 1944 destroyed 80 per cent of Zara, and the factory with it. Pietro Luxardo and his brother Nicolò, with Nicolò's wife, were killed by Tito's partisans. Giorgio Luxardo, the only survivor of the fourth generation, fled across the Adriatic; the family story says he carried a single cherry sapling.

With Nicolò III of the fifth generation he re-founded the firm briefly in Venice, then at Torreglia in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where the first marasca orchard was planted in 1947. It now has 20,000 trees, the company is still family owned, and it marked 200 years in 2021.

producer.where: Spilinga, province of Vibo Valentia, Calabria
producer.history:
'Nduja comes from Spilinga, a hill town in the province of Vibo Valentia, at the toe of Italy. It was a poor family's sausage. After the winter slaughter the better cuts went to the landowners, and what was left, the fatty, less prized trimmings, was turned into something that would keep and feed a household.

The method is simple and bold: fatback, belly and shoulder trimmings minced very fine with dried Calabrian chilli, around a third of the weight, plus salt, packed into a natural casing, lightly smoked over local wood and aged for several months. The result is soft enough to spread like a pâté and melts into anything warm.

Where it came from is argued. One theory says the Aragonese brought it in the sixteenth century; another derives it from the French andouille, introduced when Joachim Murat ruled the Kingdom of Naples at the beginning of the nineteenth century. If that second theory is right, the 'nduja in our white beans and the andouille in our gumbo share a French ancestor, a pleasing thought for a New Orleans table, offered as a theory and no more.

producer.history:
Burrata is a fresh cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, made from cow's milk, rennet and cream: a pouch of mozzarella filled with shreds of curd soaked in cream. Its birthplace is the town of Andria, though the date is argued. Some place it about 1900, at the farm of the brothers Lorenzo and Vincenzo Bianchino; more recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm with first making it in 1956.

The story told in Puglia is of a heavy February snowfall that kept Bianchino from the market. With milk that would not keep, he wrapped curd, scraps of mozzarella and the cream from the morning milking inside a skin of mozzarella, so nothing was wasted.

For decades it stayed a local fresh cheese that had to be eaten within days. In November 2016 Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication, an IGP, recognising the town's claim.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada it does what mozzarella does in a caprese: a cool, milky foil for raw Louisiana tomatoes, torn and served at room temperature.
facts: Burrata is a fresh cow's milk cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, mozzarella filled with cream-soaked curd.
Its birthplace is Andria; some date it to about 1900 at the Bianchino brothers' farm.
More recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm, in 1956.
The story says a February snowfall kept him from market, so he used up curd and cream.
Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication in November 2016.
notes: Say boo-RAH-tah: mozzarella with a creamy centre, from Andria in Puglia.

Tell the snowstorm story as a story; the date itself is argued.
No meat is printed on the dish; vegetarian and dairy questions still go to the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Burrata, boo-RAH-tah, from Andria in Puglia: a pouch of mozzarella with a soft, creamy centre, beside our Creole tomatoes.

producer.where: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María, Cádiz, Spain
producer.history:
Sherry is the fortified wine of a triangle of towns in the province of Cádiz, in southern Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María. It is made mostly from the Palomino grape, in styles from pale, salty Manzanilla and fino to the darker Amontillado and oloroso, which age in contact with air and turn nutty and deep.

What makes Sherry is the way it ages, criaderas y solera. Barrels are stacked in tiers; wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest, which is topped up from the next oldest, and so on up to the youngest. Every bottle is a blend of many years, and the style stays the same from decade to decade. That ageing was long reserved to the three towns.

In 1933 Jerez became the first denominación de origen recognised under Spain's new wine law, D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, though Rioja, which set up its own in 1925, also claims to be first.

Brennan's has finished its turtle soup with sherry for a long time: its own published recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg, and says the flavour is heightened by a touch of sherry. Tonight's menu prints aged Sherry, and which bottle the kitchen uses is a question for lineup.
facts: Sherry must come from the triangle of Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María.
D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, recognised in 1933, was the first under Spain's wine law; Rioja dates its own to 1925.
It ages by criaderas y solera, a tiered blend of young into old wine.
It is made mostly from Palomino, from Manzanilla and fino to Amontillado and oloroso.
Brennan's published turtle soup recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg.
The wine list's Sherries are Barbadillo Pale Cream, Valdespino VOS Solera 1842 and La Cigarrera Manzanilla.
notes: Say aged Sherry, the nutty fortified wine of Jerez, lifts the soup at the end; do not name a bottle until the kitchen does.
Never say the soup uses a Sherry from the wine list; that is unconfirmed.
Tell guests who avoid alcohol that Sherry is in the soup; never promise it cooks off.
A guest who likes the note can be offered a glass of the list's Sherry alongside, checked with the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Finished with aged Sherry from Jerez in southern Spain, nutty and dry, which cuts the richness of the turtle soup.
askKitchen: Which Sherry finishes the Turtle Soup, and is it added in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table?

producer.history:
Madeira is a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, discovered by the navigators João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira in 1419. The first settlers planted vines, and by the 16th century the island had a wine trade, its casks shipped across the Atlantic.

Those voyages made the wine. Casks carried across the equator in hot holds came back changed, concentrated, darker and more stable, and the islanders learned to reproduce the voyage at home. The wine is fortified with grape spirit, then aged either by canteiro, casks warmed by the sun in lofts for years, or by estufagem, tanks heated to at most 50°C for at least 90 days, a method pioneered in 1794 by Pantaleão Fernandes. The four noble grapes name the styles, from dry Sercial and medium-dry Verdelho to Bual and sweet Malmsey, from Malvasia.

Because it has already been heated and aired, Madeira keeps, for decades and even after opening, which made it the wine of the American colonies; the signers are said to have toasted the Declaration of Independence with it in 1776, a story often told but thinly documented.

In the kitchen that same caramel, walnut and sharp acidity reduces into a glaze for the broccolini on the Creole Hanger Steak.
facts: The island was discovered by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira in 1419.
Heat in ships' holds crossing the equator improved the wine; makers learned to reproduce it.
Estufagem heats the wine to at most 50°C for at least 90 days, pioneered in 1794.
Canteiro ages casks warmed naturally by the sun for years.
Already heated and oxidised, Madeira keeps for decades, even after opening.
The four noble styles: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey, from dry to sweet.
The signers are said to have toasted the Declaration of Independence with Madeira in 1776; tell it as a story.
notes: Say the broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the Portuguese island wine that is heated as it ages, so it tastes of caramel and walnut.
Never say the glaze uses a bottle from the wine list; the cooking Madeira is not named.
Guests who avoid alcohol should know the glaze is made with wine; never promise it cooks off.
A guest who loves the note can be pointed to the list's Madeiras, Broadbent and Henriques & Henriques, through the sommelier.
producer.sayIt: Broccolini glazed with Madeira, the Portuguese island wine aged in heat, beloved of the American colonies: caramel, walnut, bright acidity.
askKitchen: Which Madeira, and which style, goes into the broccolini glaze?

producer.who: The Brennan's pastry kitchen (chocolate maker not named)
producer.history:
The Snickers is Brennan's grown-up version of the candy bar, and the menu prints it plainly: Bavarian milk chocolate, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts, at $15. It appears on the dessert menu and as a choice on the Taste of Brennan's tasting menu, where a diner listing describes it as house made.

Bavarian, on a pastry menu, most often names a preparation rather than a place: a Bavarian cream, or bavarois, is a set custard lightened with whipped cream, between a mousse and a custard. Read that way, the line promises a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, not chocolate made in Bavaria. No public source names the chocolate the pastry kitchen melts into it, and no claim should be made about a maker.

The kitchen's pastry roots are real. Kris Padalino became executive chef in June 2025 after eight years at Brennan's as pastry chef and executive sous chef. Who builds The Snickers now, and with which chocolate, are questions for lineup.

Peanuts are printed on the dish: dietary questions go to the kitchen before ordering.
Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatine; vegetarian questions go to the kitchen.

producer.history:
Grand Isle is the barrier island at the southern edge of Jefferson Parish. Its oyster industry was about 150 years old when it failed in the 1980s.

The revival began in 2012, when Jules Melancon, a multigenerational oysterman, became the first permitted to farm oysters off-bottom there: seed grown in floating cages just below the surface instead of on the seabed. Others followed, working in the Grand Isle Aquapark, where ocean and estuary water mix and the salinity suits a briny oyster. Melancon died in 2023.

In April 2025 the Jefferson Parish Economic Development Commission, JEDCO, gathered eight of the island's growers under one regional brand, Grand Isle Jewels. The name nods to the island's pirate past and to Melancon himself. The brand sells to restaurants across the Southeast and Texas, and a distribution partnership with Inland Foods followed a market test of about 10,000 products.
facts: Grand Isle Jewels is a regional oyster brand launched by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish Economic Development Commission, in April 2025.
Eight Grand Isle growers farm under the brand, in floating cages rather than on the seabed.

The island's oyster industry, about 150 years old, had failed in the 1980s before off-bottom farming revived it.
Seed oysters grow just below the surface in an aquapark chosen for temperature, water flow and salinity.
The growers describe the flavour as briny and bright, from the mix of ocean and estuary water.
Inland Foods tested about 10,000 Grand Isle Jewels products before expanding distribution across the Southeast and Texas.
notes: The menu prints Grand Isle Jewel; the brand is Grand Isle Jewels. Either is fine aloud.
Expect these to taste saltier and brighter than the cooked Louisiana Oysters: they are grown in briny water on purpose.
Do not name a single farm, or say the method was invented on Grand Isle; say the island revived its oysters by farming them off the bottom.
Raw shellfish questions go to the manager or the kitchen; point to the asterisk on the menu, never give a safety verdict yourself.
producer.sayIt: These are Grand Isle Jewels, farmed in floating cages off Louisiana's barrier island: briny, bright and served raw.
askKitchen: How many oysters come per order, and which Grand Isle farm or farms are they from tonight?
Do we buy them from the growers or through a distributor?

producer.who: Louisiana oyster leases and public reefs
producer.where: Louisiana coast, from the Mississippi delta west to Vermilion Bay
producer.history:
Louisiana leads the nation in oysters. Between 2003 and 2022 it landed about a third of all oysters in the United States, and in 2022 it produced more than seven million pounds of oyster meat.

Oystermen have long dredged from two kinds of water bottom: about 1.7 million acres of public reefs, which the state opens each season, and about 400,403 acres of private leases, beds that families rent from the state and tend themselves. For years the split was roughly even. Since about 2007, freshwater pouring onto the main public grounds east of the Mississippi has weakened those reefs, and private leases now give more than nine oysters in ten; in 2023 public reefs gave only 7.3% of landings.

The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission sets the public season each year from its biologists' stock assessment, usually opening in September, with market oysters for sale following. Gulf water is less salty than the Atlantic, partly thanks to the Mississippi, which is why Louisiana oysters are plump, mild and a little sweet.
facts: From 2003 through 2022 Louisiana landed 32.3% of the nation's oysters, more than any other state.
Louisiana has about 1.7 million acres of public oyster reefs and about 400,403 acres of private leases.
In 2023 private leases gave 92.7% of Louisiana's commercial oyster landings and public reefs 7.3%.
Since about 2007 freshwater has weakened the main public grounds east of the Mississippi River.
The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission sets the public season yearly from LDWF biologists' stock assessment.
Gulf oysters grow in less salty water than Atlantic ones, so they are milder, plumper and slightly sweet.
notes: Say Louisiana oysters, grown on the state's private leases and public reefs; do not name a bay, reef or family unless the kitchen tells you.
Guests from the East Coast often ask why these are cooked: Gulf oysters are large and mild, so New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw.
If a guest wants a briny raw oyster, steer them to the Grand Isle Jewels.
Never promise the oysters in a cooked dish are local on a given night; the menu prints Louisiana, the source behind it is the kitchen's.
producer.sayIt: These are Louisiana oysters, big and mild from the Gulf, cooked in our New Orleans BBQ sauce.
askKitchen: Where are tonight's cooked oysters from, and how many come per order?

producer.history:
Shrimp is Louisiana's most valuable commercial fishery and the state is first in the nation for shrimp landings: in 2012 nearly 102 million pounds came ashore, worth more than $146 million at the dock. About 5,500 licensed shrimpers work two species, the brown shrimp of the spring season, roughly May to July, and the white shrimp of the autumn season, from mid-August to mid-December. The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission opens and closes each area on its biologists' advice.

The fishery is old and many-voiced. By the 1880s the marshes south of New Orleans were dotted with villages on stilts where shrimp were dried on raised platforms for Asia, the Philippines and Hawaii; at the peak, between 1900 and 1915, there were at least 95. Most of the merchants were Chinese, and the fishermen were Filipino, Chinese, Japanese, Italian, Croatian, Isleño, Creole, Cajun, African American and Native American. Manila Village, built over the oyster reefs of Barataria Bay by Filipino fishermen led by Quintin de la Cruz, even had its own post office.

Today almost 90 percent of the shrimp eaten in America is imported, which is what makes the word Louisiana on a menu worth saying.
facts: Louisiana is first in the nation for commercial shrimp landings; in 2012 nearly 102 million pounds were landed.
Two species carry the fishery: brown shrimp, Farfantepenaeus aztecus, and white shrimp, Litopenaeus setiferus.
Brown shrimp season generally runs May to July; white shrimp season mid-August to mid-December.
Shrimp is Louisiana's most valuable commercial fishery, with about 5,500 licensed commercial shrimpers.
At the peak of shrimp drying, 1900 to 1915, the marshes held at least 95 platform communities.
Manila Village in Barataria Bay was founded by Filipino fishermen led by Quintin de la Cruz.
Almost 90 percent of the shrimp eaten in the United States is imported, which is why Louisiana on a menu matters.
Louisiana's Act 372 of 2019 requires a menu notice when a restaurant serves imported shrimp or crawfish.
notes: Use the menu's words: Louisiana shrimp on the Shrimp & Grits and the Roost Popcorn Shrimp, Gulf shrimp on the children's fried shrimp.
If asked brown or white, the honest answer depends on the season and the boat; ask the kitchen rather than guess.
Never say all our shrimp are Louisiana: the children's breakfast popcorn shrimp prints no origin.
A good story at the table: the Filipino and Chinese shrimp-drying villages of the marsh, more than a century ago.
producer.sayIt: It's wild Louisiana shrimp, from the state that lands more shrimp than any other in the country.
askKitchen: Are tonight's shrimp brown or white, and from which supplier?

producer.history:
Louisiana runs the largest commercial blue crab fishery in the Gulf and in the United States, supplying about a quarter of all the blue crab caught in the country. In 2018 it landed 30.6% of the nation's blue crabs, and its 2024 harvest was 40 million pounds. The crab is trapped in the brackish marshes and bays where fresh river water meets the Gulf.

Most of that catch is cooked and picked by hand, and the meat is sold by grade. New Orleans seafood counters sell three: jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw. Lump is prized for its large, sweet white pieces that hold their shape on a plate, while claw meat, darker and sweeter, is what many home cooks put in stuffed crabs.

Brennan's prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Crab & Corn Omelette, Louisiana crab on the Gulf Fish en Papillote, and serves warm Louisiana Crab Claws as a starter. No picking house or crabber is named.
facts: Louisiana's commercial blue crab fishery is the largest in the Gulf and in the United States.
Louisiana supplies about a quarter of the blue crab harvested in the United States.

producer.history:
Gulf fish on a New Orleans menu means the day's catch, not one species. The city's appetite runs to fish such as true American red snapper and black drum, which sell far above the national average here, and sheepshead, an estuarine fish of Louisiana's coast that is nearly all sold to restaurants and markets in the state.

Louisiana has worked to widen that list. In 1981 the legislature created the Louisiana Seafood Promotion and Marketing Board to promote the state's commercial catch, with particular attention to underused species.

Brennan's owner has a public record on Gulf seafood. After the 2010 BP oil spill Ralph Brennan testified before Congress about the damage to the Gulf seafood industry, and he advocates sustainable, local seafood sourcing in each of his restaurants. In New Orleans the Audubon Nature Institute runs GULF, a sustainable seafood programme founded in 2012 that works with restaurants and fisheries.
facts: Gulf fish means the day's catch from Gulf waters, not a fixed species.
True American red snapper and black drum sell far above average in the New Orleans area.
Nearly all commercially caught Louisiana sheepshead is sold to restaurants or markets in the state.

Never guess a species. If the kitchen has not said, offer to ask.

producer.where: Gulf of Mexico; farmed redfish mainly in Texas
producer.history:
Redfish, the red drum, was an important commercial and restaurant fish in Louisiana until 1988. Its fall began one March evening in 1980, when Paul Prudhomme served blackened redfish at K-Paul's in New Orleans; from 1983 he took it on pop-ups to New York and San Francisco, where people queued for hours. Kitchens all over the country copied it, and the Gulf was fished hard: 12.7 million pounds of red drum in a single year.

The stock fell, and Louisiana's Wildlife and Fisheries Commission closed the commercial redfish fishery in the late 1980s; sources give 1987 and 1988. In 1988 anglers were limited to five fish a day with only one over 27 inches, and there has been no commercial redfish fishing in Louisiana since.

The collapse also spurred red drum hatcheries and farms, partly to restock the Gulf, and Texas has led the nation in red drum farms. Louisiana law lets licensed dealers sell farm-raised red drum, or red drum legally caught and sold commercially outside the state, so the redfish on a Louisiana menu today is one or the other.
facts: Paul Prudhomme served blackened redfish at K-Paul's in March 1980 and set off a national craze.
In one year 12.7 million pounds of red drum were harvested from the Gulf.
Louisiana closed commercial redfish fishing in the late 1980s; sources date the ban to 1987 or 1988.
Louisiana's 1988 rules cut anglers to five redfish a day, only one over 27 inches; commercial redfish fishing has not returned.
Louisiana law lets licensed dealers sell farm-raised red drum, or red drum legally caught commercially outside the state.
Red drum farming grew from the 1980s collapse; in one national count Texas led with eight red drum farms.
notes: Redfish is the red drum: firm, mild, slightly sweet, with a black spot near the tail.
Never say ours is wild Louisiana redfish: Louisiana has had no commercial redfish fishery since the late 1980s.
The story guests enjoy: Prudhomme's blackening craze nearly fished redfish out, and the rules since brought it back.
Where ours comes from, farmed or another state's catch, is a chef question.
producer.sayIt: Redfish is the red drum, firm and mild; it is the fish Paul Prudhomme made famous, and here it stands in for the classic sole.
askKitchen: Is our redfish farm-raised, and from where?

producer.who: Louisiana crawfish farmers and Atchafalaya fishermen
producer.where: South Louisiana rice country and the Atchafalaya Basin
producer.history:
Louisiana grows nearly all of America's crawfish. Its crawfish ponds covered 120,654 acres in 1990 and about 225,789 acres in a recent count, against roughly 7,500 acres in the whole of the rest of the country.

More than half of that farming happens in rice fields. After the rice harvest in July and August the farmers flood the same fields as crawfish ponds, so the clay soil that suits rice gives a second crop in the cooler months. Farm-raised crawfish make up most of Louisiana's supply, about 80% by one count.

The rest is wild, trapped in the deeper water of the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States, which has historically given about 90% of the state's wild landings.

On the Roost menu the Crawfish Meat Pies come with a chive rémoulade. The menu does not print Louisiana, so whether the tail meat in them is Louisiana crawfish is a question for the kitchen; Louisiana law requires a menu notice when imported crawfish are served.
facts: Louisiana crawfish ponds grew from 120,654 acres in 1990 to 225,789 acres, against about 7,500 acres elsewhere in the US.
More than half of Louisiana's crawfish farming is done in rice fields flooded after the rice harvest.
Farm-raised crawfish are about 80% of Louisiana's crawfish industry by one count; the rest is trapped wild.
Wild crawfish are trapped in the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States.
About 90% of Louisiana's wild crawfish landings have historically come from the Atchafalaya Basin.
Louisiana's Act 372 of 2019 requires a menu notice when imported crawfish or shrimp are served.
notes: The menu prints Crawfish Meat Pies, not Louisiana crawfish; do not add the word until the kitchen confirms it.
A good line: most Louisiana crawfish grow in rice fields, a second crop after the rice harvest.

producer.sayIt: Crawfish are Louisiana's own: most are raised in flooded rice fields, the rest trapped wild in the Atchafalaya swamp.

producer.where: Louisiana, from licensed turtle farms and collectors
producer.history:
Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s, and it is still on the menus of the old houses: Arnaud's, Commander's Palace, Mandina's, Felix's and Brennan's among them. At Brennan's the chefs use snappers, freshwater snapping turtles.

The rules on which snapper changed in 2004. The alligator snapping turtle, the great loggerhead once common in Louisiana markets, became off limits to commercial trappers when a Wildlife and Fisheries regulation took effect on 20 November 2004. Licensed turtle farmers may still sell alligator snappers hatched from their own breeding stock, and Commander's Palace uses farm-raised alligator snapper for a steady supply. The common snapping turtle could still be taken and sold by holders of a reptile and amphibian collection licence, by a 2017 account, and most of the state's turtle trade involves farm-hatched animals.

For cooks, Brennan's own published turtle soup recipe notes that fresh or frozen turtle meat can be bought from specialty markets and seafood dealers in and around New Orleans. Brennan's menu prints 100% turtle meat, which means the meat in the soup is all turtle, not stretched with veal or beef. It does not say which snapper or which supplier.

Louisiana banned commercial trapping of the wild alligator snapping turtle from 20 November 2004.

notes: Say 100% turtle meat, exactly as printed, and explain it means no veal or beef in the soup.

Never the courtyard turtles: they are red-eared sliders, pardoned house mascots, and the chefs use snappers. Smile when guests joke about it.

producer.history:
George Leidenheimer came to New Orleans from Deidesheim in Germany and opened a bakery on Dryades Street in 1896. He began with the heavy, dense brown breads of home, but the city's customers of French descent preferred a light, airy loaf, so he turned to New Orleans French bread, with its crisp crust.

In 1904 the bakery moved to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes. Its bread is older than the po-boy itself, which dates to the late 1920s, yet it became the loaf most of the city's po-boy shops reach for, and Leidenheimer is now the largest and best-known po-boy bread maker in New Orleans. The dough is naturally fermented and hand-stretched to a 32-inch loaf, and the bakery also makes pistolets and muffuletta bread.

The family still runs it: Robert J. "Sandy" Whann IV, George Leidenheimer's great-grandson, is the fourth generation and runs it with his sister, Katherine. After Hurricane Katrina, when the city had no power or clean water, Whann kept the bread coming by sending his operations manager to bake in a friend's bakery in Chicago.

Moved in 1904 to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes.

Its bread predates the po-boy, which dates to the late 1920s.

producer.where: West Bank, Jefferson Parish (Marrero and Harvey addresses); co-op in New Orleans East
producer.history:
Tien Dat is a small local tofu maker, part of the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, whose extra firm tofu reaches the city through the co-op. Tien Dat Tofu LLC is registered on the West Bank, with addresses in Marrero and Harvey, across the river from the French Quarter. The tofu is made fresh in small batches, sold as extra firm and in flavoured styles such as black mushroom, and lemongrass and red chilli.

VEGGI stands for the Village de L'Est Green Growers Initiative. Village de L'Est is the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East, and the co-op was established there in 2011, across the street from Mary Queen of Vietnam Church, in the aftermath of the BP oil spill, when twelve growers and programme developers chose through a community forum to build jobs in urban agriculture. It is owned and run by its members.

The co-op sells herbs, vegetables, chilli oil and more at the Crescent City Farmers Market, but it is best known for its freshly made tofu. Printing the name on the Blackened Tofu ties Brennan's plate to that community.

producer.history:
Two Brooks Farm sits at Sumner in the Mississippi Delta. Mike Wagner started it in 1992, and he is a ninth-generation farmer: his family counts an unbroken line of ten generations back to 1742. The farm grows about 2,000 acres of rice and 1,000 of soybeans.

What sets it apart is the birds. The farm lies on the flyway, and after harvest ducks and geese settle on the flooded fields. Wagner noticed his soil changing where they gathered and began cutting back on fertiliser; the birds now supply much of it, and no fungicides or insecticides go on the rice.

From that long-grain rice the family built a line of 14 products, rice, grits and flour among them, with the Original Mississippi Midlands Brown Rice Grits one of Wagner's favourites. His son Lawrence and daughter Abbey, the next generation, have helped widen the range, and the products reach restaurants through US Foods. In 2022 Wagner was named Mississippi's winner of the Swisher Sweets/Sunbelt Ag Expo Southeastern Farmer of the Year award.

Wagner is a ninth-generation farmer; the family traces ten generations back to 1742.
Ducks and geese winter on the fields and supply much of the fertiliser.

A line of 14 products, including rice, grits and flour.

producer.who: Mushroom Maggie's Farm (to be confirmed by the chef)
producer.history:
Mushroom Maggie's Farm is the best-known Louisiana grower called Maggie's, and the likely source of the side the menu prints simply as Maggie's Mushrooms. No public source names Brennan's as a customer, so treat the link as likely, not settled.

The farm is in St Francisville, upriver from Baton Rouge. Maggie Long and her husband Cyrus Lester have owned and run it since 2018. Their start was hard: in 2017, in the first week of official operations, a propane hose burst while they were steaming fruiting blocks, the barn burned down and Lester was left with burns over seventy percent of his skin. They started again from nothing and spent the next year rebuilding, so 2018 became the farm's first real year.

Today the farm grows 1,200 to 1,500 pounds of mushrooms a week, at least eight kinds, among them lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut. It supplies about twenty top New Orleans restaurants and many closer to home, and Maggie Long often works directly with chefs as they plan their menus.

producer.where: Reserve, Louisiana (founded on Tchoupitoulas Street, New Orleans)
producer.history:
In 1923 Alvin A. Baumer borrowed money from his future in-laws and bought Mill's Fruit Products, a small snow-cone syrup company on Tchoupitoulas Street. Tucked in a drawer was a recipe for a pepper sauce labelled Crystal Pure. Baumer renamed it Crystal Pure Louisiana Hot Sauce and began bottling it in the city.

For decades Baumer Foods was as much a maker of jellies, preserves and mustard as of hot sauce. From the 1940s it bottled Crystal on Tulane Avenue, where a neon sign of a chef stirring a steaming pot of strawberry jam became a local landmark. The flooding after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ruined that plant and forced the company to drop its historic preserves, jellies and mustard; it moved upriver to Reserve, Louisiana, at the Port of South Louisiana, 9 feet above sea level.

The recipe is short: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt, giving a reddish orange sauce with medium heat. The company is still family owned, led by Alvin "Al" Baumer Jr.

producer.history:
Abita Brewing was founded in 1986 by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming in downtown Abita Springs, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain. Its first beer went on sale on 4 July that year in New Orleans and Mandeville, and it is described as the first craft brewery to open in the South.

Amber was one of the brewery's original beers, and the one that put it on the map. Patton wrote the recipes for the flagships, Amber, Turbo Dog, Purple Haze and the root beer among them, before selling his share in 1997. Amber is a Munich-style lager of pale and caramel malts with German Perle hops: smooth, malty and lightly caramel, at 4.5 percent and a low 17 IBU.

At Brennan's the Amber goes into the Mimolette fondue of the Shells & Cheese, where its malt and low bitterness suit a cheese sauce, and the dessert list pours Abita Root Beer in the Amarula float.

producer.where: 240 Pelican Avenue, Algiers Point, New Orleans
producer.history:
Congregation Coffee was started in 2015 by two partners who met while working at Cochon Butcher. The name is a local joke and a hope at once: a group of alligators is called a congregation, and the blends High Walk, Low Walk and Gallop are named for an alligator's gaits. Two years after the roastery began, the café opened in a Victorian storefront at 240 Pelican Avenue in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter.

Brennan's was a customer long before it was an owner. By 2023 the restaurant had poured Congregation for seven years, and the buyer called them the best roasters in the city. When the company ceased operations that year while looking for new owners, it came under Brennan ownership, and in November 2023 the Algiers Point café and the wholesale roastery on Tchoupitoulas Street reopened, with a founder collaborating. A second café followed at Magazine Street and Jefferson Avenue.

So the coffee at Brennan's comes from a roaster in the family: the Traditional Breakfast tasting pours Brennan's Private Blend Congregation Coffee & Chicory beside the Bananas Foster, and the coffee list prints a Single Estate-grown Congregation Coffee, Roasted For Brennan's.

producer.where: St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans, and Louisiana generally
producer.history:
Creole is a growers' word before it is a variety. Farmers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes traditionally sold their tomatoes as Creole, and said that ripening on the vine in rich alluvial river soil gave them a flavour no other Louisiana or American tomato had. In the early 1900s, before tomatoes carried variety names, fruit from St. Charles, St. John and St. James parishes was simply called Creole too.

The LSU AgCenter muddied the water in 1969, when researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety actually named Creole. It yielded poorly, less than six pounds a plant, was never common in St. Bernard or Plaquemines, and the AgCenter did not keep its seed. So a Creole tomato today is a Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not one cultivar.

The city celebrates it every June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival, which began in 1985 to mark the start of the season and honours the farmers who grow them. The French Market itself has stood since 1791.

producer.who: Louisiana cane syrup (Steen's of Abbeville is the best-known maker; the menu names none)
producer.history:
Louisiana cane syrup is cane juice concentrated by long cooking in open kettles, with nothing taken out and nothing added. Slow Food lists traditional cane syrup on its Ark of Taste, the catalogue of heritage foods worth saving.

The name most Louisianans reach for is Steen's. In 1910 an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane crop near Abbeville. Rather than lose it, he built a small mill and turned the frozen cane into a few barrels of syrup. By 1930 Charley and Elizabeth Steen and their children had built a larger mill in the heart of Abbeville, on the banks of Bayou Vermilion, and from the 1950s the yellow can became a fixture of Cajun and Creole kitchens. The mill is still run by the Steen family and still cooks in open kettles, which is why the label reads 100% Pure Cane Syrup.

Brennan's menu prints cane syrup on the peaches of the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast but names no maker, so Steen's is the story of the style, not a claim about the kitchen's bottle.

producer.who: Roasted chicory root, the New Orleans coffee tradition
producer.where: Grown mostly in France and Belgium; roasted and blended with coffee in New Orleans
producer.history:
Chicory is the root of a blue-flowered perennial, dug, cut, dried, roasted and ground. In 1806 the British blockaded the French coast and Napoleon answered with his Continental System, an embargo on British trade that lasted until 1814. Imported coffee grew scarce, chicory became the French substitute, and the French kept their taste for it after the embargo ended. The habit reached New Orleans with its French colonial ties.

New Orleans was ready for it. By 1840 the port was the second largest coffee importer in the United States. During the Civil War, from 1861, the Union naval blockade cut the port off, and Louisianans stretched what coffee they had with chicory. Smithsonian calls it a cost-saving workaround that stuck around for tradition's sake: the rest of the South dropped it, New Orleans did not.

Today most commercial chicory is grown in France and Belgium. At Brennan's it is in the New Orleans Style Coffee, a blend of chicory and dark roast, in the private blend poured on the breakfast tasting, and baked into the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.

notes: Chicory is not coffee: it is a roasted root blended with coffee for body and a roasty, bitter-chocolate depth.

The breakfast tasting blend is roasted by Congregation, which has its own card; the menu names no roaster for the New Orleans Style Coffee, and where the chicory is grown is not public, so name no country for ours.
The Civil War story is true but not the whole story: the French habit came first.

producer.where: Louisiana and the Mississippi valley; Oak Alley Plantation, St. James Parish, for the first grafted pecans
producer.history:
Louisiana is one of the few states where the pecan is native. The state holds between 19,000 and 21,000 acres of native trees, and their nuts tend to be small, flavourful and high in oil, unlike the larger improved varieties bred since. The LSU AgCenter runs the only university research station in the country devoted solely to pecans.

The improved pecan itself began in Louisiana. In the winter of 1846 or 1847, Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, grafted pecan wood from a tree with large, thin-shelled nuts onto other trees. He grafted sixteen trees near the house, more were grafted later, and by the end of the Civil War in 1865 Oak Alley had 126 grafted trees in bearing. His nut, later named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, and grafting made the pecan an orchard crop.

In New Orleans kitchens the pecan stands where the almond stood in French recipes. It runs right through Brennan's menus: the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the oat and pecan crumble on the Baked Apple, the pecans on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and the pralines on the bread pudding.

producer.who: The New Orleans praline and the pralinières
producer.history:
The praline began as a French sugared almond, named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, whose chef made it. Early in the eighteenth century the Ursuline nuns are credited with bringing the candy to New Orleans.

The New Orleans praline is a different thing, and it was made by the city's Black women. They took the almond sweet, used the pecans that grew all around them and added milk or cream, turning a hard sugared nut into the soft, creamy patty the city knows.

In the mid to late nineteenth century, women called pralinières sold them on the streets of the French Quarter. Free women of colour and enslaved women alike made and sold them, and for Black women it was a way to earn their own money; some bought their own freedom and their families' with the proceeds. On Brennan's New Orleans Bread Pudding, pralines bring that history and a caramel crunch to the whiskey caramel and buttermilk ice cream.

producer.who: Louisiana popcorn rice (the Della type, bred by the LSU AgCenter)
producer.where: LSU Rice Research Station, Crowley, Louisiana; milled across south Louisiana
producer.history:
Popcorn rice is Louisiana's own aromatic long grain. The Rice Research Station at Crowley opened in 1909 on a 60-acre farm, set up by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station with the USDA and now run by the LSU AgCenter, and it was the AgCenter that released Della, an aromatic long-grain rice bred for cooks who wanted a fluffy texture and a strong popcorn-like aroma. Della is tall, falls over easily and yields poorly, which is why it remains a speciality rather than a field staple. The aroma itself is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the molecule that also scents basmati, jasmine and fresh popcorn.

The best-known retail example comes from the Conrad Rice Mill in New Iberia, founded in 1912 by Philip Amalus Conrad and the oldest independently owned rice mill in the United States still working. Its Konriko brand, named in the 1950s, sells Wild Pecan Rice, a Della-type brown popcorn rice that smells of roasted nuts. Mike Davis bought the mill in February 1975 and turned it towards speciality rice.

Brennan's prints popcorn rice under its Seafood Gumbo and names no mill, so Konriko is the story of the style, not the kitchen's bag.

producer.where: The southwest Louisiana prairie, centred on Crowley, Acadia Parish
producer.history:
South Louisiana Rice Dressing carries its place in its name. Rice growing on the southwest Louisiana prairie began in earnest in the early 1880s, and by 1890 a record crop of 80 million pounds made Louisiana the leading rice state, overtaking South Carolina. Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish, became the centre of the industry, its fields watered by canals and wells.

Between 1800 and 1920 the region changed from subsistence farming and open-range cattle country into the first mechanised commercial rice region in the world, and southwest Louisiana still holds nearly 500,000 acres of rice land.

That is why rice, not bread, is the stuffing of south Louisiana: rice dressing is cooked rice folded into browned meat and the holy trinity, a Sunday and holiday dish. Brennan's prints the side with no description and no rice brand, so the meats and the rice are questions for the kitchen.

producer.who: LaPlace andouille, the Andouille Capital of the World
producer.where: LaPlace, St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana
producer.history:
Andouille in Louisiana is a River Parishes sausage. The Germans of the German Coast, upriver from New Orleans, brought a strong tradition of sausage making, with French, Acadian, Native American, Spanish and African influences alongside. The town that made it famous is LaPlace, which Governor Edwin Edwards proclaimed the Andouille Capital of the World in the 1970s.

Three LaPlace shops carry the name. Jacob's World Famous Andouille dates from 1928, when Nelson and Camille Jacob began selling smoked andouille from their Milesville home; Aaron Lion is its fourth-generation owner. Wayne Jacob's Smokehouse, no relation to Jacob's, opened in 1950, and Bailey's sits next door to Jacob's. Locals say Jacob's is the smokiest, Wayne Jacob's has the spice and the girth, and Bailey's sits in between. LaPlace andouille is, as one writer put it, thick as a wrist, brown as tobacco and steeped in pecan wood smoke.

The town has held an Andouille Festival every October since the first, on 28 and 29 October 1972. Brennan's prints andouille in its Seafood Gumbo, as in its published gumbo recipe, and names no maker.

producer.who: Tasso, the Cajun smokehouse seasoning meat
producer.history:
Tasso belongs to the boucherie, the communal hog butchering of Acadiana, where neighbours killed a pig together and shared every part. The boucherie gave the Cajun larder boudin, cracklin', andouille and tasso, and tasso was traditionally made from the last lean pieces: a seasoning meat, not a meal.

It is often called a ham, but the name misleads. Tasso is cut from the shoulder, not the hind leg. The shoulder is sliced across the grain into pieces about three inches thick, cured briefly in salt and sugar for only three or four hours, rinsed, rubbed with cayenne and garlic, and hot-smoked until cooked through. The smokehouse has its own Acadian French word, boucanière.

Cooks rarely eat tasso on its own. They dice it into jambalaya, stews and braised vegetables, where a little carries smoke, salt and heat through the pot. At Brennan's it seasons the Creole sauce of the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. The menu names no maker, so who smokes it is a question for the kitchen.

producer.where: New Orleans company, headquartered in Metairie; distilled at Buffalo Trace, Frankfort, Kentucky
producer.founded: The Sazerac Company: 1869, from the Sazerac Coffee House of the 1850s
producer.history:
Sazerac Rye carries the name of a bar. In the 1850s the Sazerac Coffee House in New Orleans took its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, which by the company's account went into its house cocktail. Thomas H. Handy took over the coffee house in 1869, and as phylloxera ruined the European vineyards, rye whiskey took the cognac's place in the city's drink.

The bottle is the Sazerac Company's namesake straight rye, distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky, and bottled at 90 proof. It was once labelled 6 years old and now carries no age statement; the mash bill is not disclosed, and it shares its grain recipe with Sazerac 18 Year and Thomas H. Handy. Reviewers find it light bodied for a rye, with apricot, orange peel, caramel and vanilla over the pepper.

The company grew from Handy's firm, which also came to own Antoine Peychaud's bitters. It was reorganised as the Sazerac Company in 1919, rode out Prohibition as a grocery wholesaler, and in 1948 was bought by Magnolia Liquor, a New Orleans wholesaler founded by two partners; the family of one of them owns it still. It bought Herbsaint in 1949 and the distillery now called Buffalo Trace in 1992, and it remains privately held, headquartered in Metairie, with more than 500 brands. All three bottles of the Classic Sazerac are its own.

In 2019 it opened the Sazerac House at the corner of Canal and Magazine, a museum with a small still that makes Sazerac rye.
facts: Named, like the company and the cocktail, for the Sazerac Coffee House of the 1850s, itself named for Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac.
A 90 proof straight rye distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky; once labelled 6 years old, it now carries no age statement.
The mash bill is not disclosed; it shares its grain recipe with Sazerac 18 Year and Thomas H. Handy.
Reviewers taste apricot, orange peel, caramel and vanilla over rye pepper, in a light body.
A 100 proof Sazerac Rye and the 125 proof Sazerac Rye Full Proof are separate bottles.
The firm became the Sazerac Company in 1919 and has been privately owned since Magnolia Liquor, a New Orleans wholesaler, bought it in 1948.
The company bought the distillery now called Buffalo Trace in 1992.
The Sazerac House at Canal and Magazine opened in 2019, a museum with a small still making Sazerac rye.
The company also owns Peychaud's Bitters and Herbsaint, the other two bottles in the Classic Sazerac.
notes: Say Sazerac Rye is made by a New Orleans company and distilled at Buffalo Trace in Kentucky. The small still at the Sazerac House also makes some Sazerac rye; the standard bottle is the Kentucky one.
Guests ask whether the drink is named for the whiskey. Both the cocktail and the company take the name of the Sazerac Coffee House, which took it from a cognac.
Do not quote an age: the bottle carries none. Sazerac 18 Year, a 100 proof Sazerac Rye and Sazerac Rye Full Proof are different bottles.
If a guest asks who owns it: a privately held New Orleans family company. Name nobody.

producer.sayIt: Sazerac Rye comes from the New Orleans company named for the old Sazerac Coffee House; it is distilled at Buffalo Trace in Kentucky.
askKitchen: Is the Classic poured on the standard 90 proof Sazerac Rye, or another Sazerac bottling such as the 100 proof?

producer.where: Created on Royal Street, New Orleans; made at Buffalo Trace, Frankfort, Kentucky
producer.founded: between 1849 and 1857, by the most careful account
producer.history:
Peychaud's Bitters began with Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole apothecary from Saint-Domingue, the French colony that became Haiti, who kept his shop on Royal Street in New Orleans. The most careful account dates the bright red aromatic bitters that carry his name to between 1849 and 1857, though company tellings reach back to the 1830s. In an 1857 advertisement in the New Orleans Bee he listed the city bars that sold them, the nearby Sazerac House among them.

Hard times followed. Peychaud had to sell his Royal Street building in 1868. By one account he then licensed the formula to local pharmacists while compounding it for Thomas H. Handy of the Sazerac Coffee House; another dates Handy's purchase of the brand to 1873. Peychaud died in 1883. The bitters have belonged ever since to Handy's firm and the Sazerac Company that grew from it, the New Orleans company behind Sazerac Rye and Herbsaint.

It is a gentian based bitters, close to Angostura in kind but with a stronger anise aroma and a background of mint; the recipe is kept secret. It is bottled at 35 percent alcohol and made at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky, and the Sazerac House at Canal and Magazine also makes some bitters.

The company sells a second version, Peychaud's Barrel-Aged, launched in 2014 and rested 140 days in Sazerac Rye barrels, which adds oak, vanilla and candied spice.
facts: Created between 1849 and 1857, by the most careful account, by Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole apothecary from Saint-Domingue.
An 1857 advertisement in the New Orleans Bee listed the Sazerac House among the bars selling it.
Peychaud sold his Royal Street building in 1868; Thomas H. Handy came to own the brand in the 1870s, one source says 1873.
Gentian based, like Angostura, but with a stronger anise aroma and a background of mint.
Bottled at 35 percent alcohol and made at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky.
Peychaud's Barrel-Aged, launched in 2014, rests 140 days in Sazerac Rye barrels, adding oak, vanilla and candied spice.
Antoine Peychaud lived from 1803 to 1883.
notes: His apothecary is believed to have stood at what is now 437 Royal Street, on Brennan's block. Say believed, and tell it only once lineup has cleared it.
Never say Peychaud invented the cocktail or the word: cocktail was defined in print in 1806, when he was a small child.
The Origin Story prints barrel-aged Peychaud's. A Sazerac Company bottling exists; whether ours is that one or aged by the bar is a lineup question, so say barrel-aged and no more.
Say born on Royal Street, made in Kentucky today. Never say it is made on Royal Street.
Thompson's Dream uses Bitter Truth Creole Bitters instead, a tribute to the same style; a guest who wants Peychaud's there is asking for a change to the drink.
producer.sayIt: Peychaud's is the red New Orleans bitters Antoine Peychaud created in his Royal Street apothecary in the 1850s.
askKitchen: Is the Origin Story's barrel-aged Peychaud's the Sazerac Company's Barrel-Aged bottling, or bitters aged by our bar?
May we tell guests that Peychaud's apothecary stood on our block of Royal Street?

producer.where: New Orleans, where it was created
producer.history:
Herbsaint was born in New Orleans in 1934, just after the repeal of Prohibition, while absinthe was still banned in the United States, as it had been since 1912. Its makers were J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learnt absinthe making in France during the First World War.

Legendre first sold it as Legendre Absinthe, though it never held grand wormwood. Within months the Federal Alcohol Control Administration objected to the word absinthe, and he renamed it Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood. In time it became a usual rinse for the Sazerac, the city's own cocktail.

In June 1949 the Sazerac Company, the New Orleans firm behind Sazerac Rye and Peychaud's, bought J.M. Legendre and Co. In the mid-1950s the standard bottling became a different 90 proof recipe, and by the early 1970s it was the only Herbsaint made. In December 2009, for the brand's 75th anniversary, the company brought back Legendre's original 100 proof recipe as Herbsaint Original. Both are sold today, and the 90 proof remains the predominant bottling.

The company does not say where Herbsaint is made now, so it is described as born in New Orleans, not made there.
facts: Created in New Orleans in 1934 by J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, as an absinthe substitute.
First sold as Legendre Absinthe; federal regulators objected to the word, and it became Herbsaint.
The name comes from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood; Legendre's liqueur never held grand wormwood.
The Sazerac Company bought J.M. Legendre and Co. in June 1949.
The standard bottling is 90 proof; Herbsaint Original, Legendre's 100 proof recipe, returned in December 2009.
Absinthe was banned in the United States from 1912 until 2007.
notes: Say ERB-sant: the H is silent.
It is a rinse, not a pour: the guest gets the anise perfume without much of the flavour.
Call it New Orleans' own anise liqueur, born here in 1934. Where it is made today is not published, so never say it is made in the city.
Is it absinthe? No: it was made as a substitute while absinthe was banned. Thompson's Dream rinses with real absinthe, and the Origin Story uses one too.
Questions about what is in it go to the bar; never answer them from memory.
producer.sayIt: Herbsaint is New Orleans' own anise liqueur, created here in 1934 while absinthe was banned; it rinses the glass for aroma.
askKitchen: Do we rinse with the standard 90 proof Herbsaint or the 100 proof Herbsaint Original?

producer.history:
Distilling runs back generations in the Willett family. John David Willett, born in 1841, was a master distiller, and his son A. Lambert Willett followed him into the trade. In 1936 Lambert and his sons, led by Thompson Willett, founded the Willett Distilling Company on the family farm outside Bardstown, with Thompson as founder and president. The first batch, about 30 barrels, was made on 17 March 1937. Old Bardstown bourbon followed in the 1940s.

The stills went quiet in the early 1980s, after a brief spell making ethanol during the energy crisis of the 1970s. On 1 July 1984 Thompson Willett's son-in-law bought the property and renamed the business Kentucky Bourbon Distillers, which for years bottled whiskey distilled elsewhere. Its Willett Pot Still Reserve bourbon, launched in 2008 in a bottle shaped from the original still's blueprints, began that way too.

After years of renovation the family started the distillery again in January 2012, and its first own rye, two years old, reached the market around 2015. The Family Estate 4-year rye is a small batch, hand bottled at barrel strength, so its proof changes from batch to batch; it runs far hotter and spicier than the 90 proof Sazerac Rye of the Classic.

The first batch, about 30 barrels, was made on 17 March 1937.
The stills fell silent in the early 1980s; from 1984 the business ran as Kentucky Bourbon Distillers, long an independent bottler.
The family restarted the distillery in January 2012; its first own rye reached the market around 2015.
The Family Estate 4-year rye is a small batch, hand bottled at barrel strength; its proof varies from batch to batch.
Willett Pot Still Reserve came out in 2008 in a bottle shaped from the original still's blueprints.
notes: Thompson's Dream is the house's own name: no Willett bottle carries it and nothing published explains it. It may nod to Thompson Willett, the founder; offer that only as a guess.
Read the proof from today's bottle; barrel strength changes batch to batch, so never quote one from memory.
Willett bottled whiskey made elsewhere before 2012. Do not say where a particular bottle was distilled unless the label or the bar says so.
Name nobody from today's family or staff; say a family distillery in Bardstown since 1936.
Offer Thompson's Dream to the guest who loves the Classic: louder rye spice and more heat.
producer.sayIt: Willett is a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, since 1936; its barrel-strength rye makes Thompson's Dream bigger and spicier than the Classic.
askKitchen: What proof is the Willett 4-year rye we are pouring now?
Does the house tell a story behind the name Thompson's Dream?

producer.history:
Rittenhouse Rye was first sold in Philadelphia in 1934, just after Prohibition, by Continental Distilling, and named for the city's Rittenhouse Square. In 1948 it was relaunched as a four-year-old bottled in bond rye, the form it keeps. Heaven Hill bought the brand in the 1990s, in 1993 by some accounts and 1999 by others, and moved its production from Pennsylvania to Kentucky.

Heaven Hill itself was founded at Bardstown in 1935 by a group of investors; in time five brothers of one family bought out the rest, and their descendants own and run the company still. On 7 November 1996 fire swept through its warehouses, and some 90,000 barrels burned. In 1999 it bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville, where it has distilled since, while ageing and bottling stayed around Bardstown; a new Bardstown distillery filled its first barrel on 7 April 2025.

Bottled in bond means the spirit of a single distilling season, aged at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse and bottled at 100 proof. Rittenhouse is 51 percent rye, with corn and malted barley: a modern Kentucky recipe, lower in rye than the old Pennsylvania ryes it nods to.

Rumors are Flying prints Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye. No public source says what that means: a barrel chosen for the house, or rye rested again in a cask of the bar's own. The bar holds that story.
facts: First sold in Philadelphia in 1934 by Continental Distilling and named for Rittenhouse Square.
Relaunched in 1948 as a four-year-old bottled in bond rye.
Heaven Hill bought the brand in the 1990s (sources give 1993 or 1999) and moved production from Pennsylvania to Kentucky.
Bottled in bond: one distilling season, at least four years in a bonded warehouse, bottled at 100 proof.
The mash bill is 51 percent rye; sources split the corn and malted barley differently.
Heaven Hill was founded at Bardstown in 1935 and is still family owned and run.
Since 1999 Heaven Hill has distilled at Bernheim in Louisville, ageing and bottling around Bardstown.
A fire on 7 November 1996 swept its Bardstown warehouses, and some 90,000 barrels burned.
notes: Say barrel-aged for Brennan's, and no more, until the bar gives the story: who aged it, in what cask, and for how long.
A barrel pick is a single barrel that a bar or shop chooses at the distillery and bottles under its own label. Ask whether ours is one, or rye rested again in our own cask.
Never say Brennan's distilled it: Heaven Hill makes Rittenhouse in Kentucky.
At 100 proof its rye spice holds up against the tart cherry and brown sugar.
Heaven Hill is family owned; name nobody from the family or the distillery.
producer.sayIt: Rumors are Flying uses Rittenhouse, a 100 proof bottled in bond rye from Heaven Hill in Kentucky, in a barrel-aged version for Brennan's.
askKitchen: What is Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse: a barrel picked for the house, or Rittenhouse rested again in our own cask?
Who aged it, in what cask, and for how long?

producer.history:
Rabbit Hole was founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist who left the profession to distil whiskey. The name, by one account, comes from his wife's warning that the venture would take the family down a rabbit hole from which they could never return. She is a Louisville native and a bourbon lover who had drawn him from Scotch to bourbon, and Dareringer, the sherry-finished bourbon, is named in her honour.

In its first years the brand's whiskey was made at other distilleries while its own was designed and built. The distillery opened in May 2018 in downtown Louisville. In June 2019 Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share, at a price never disclosed; at the time the founder kept most of his shares and stayed on to run the company.

Dareringer is a wheated Kentucky straight bourbon. It ages first in new charred American oak, then is finished in casks that held Pedro Ximénez, a dark and very sweet sherry, and it is bottled at 93 proof. The finish lays raisin and dried fruit richness over the bourbon's vanilla and oak, a richness that carries the smoke, the Angostura, the orange and the cherry of the Birdcage.
facts: Founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist.
Its downtown Louisville distillery opened in May 2018.
Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share in June 2019; the founder stayed on to run the company at the time.
Dareringer is a wheated straight bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks and bottled at 93 proof.
Dareringer is named for the founder's wife, a Louisville native who drew him from Scotch to bourbon.

notes: The menu pours the Birdcage only in the Roost. From the dining room, invite a whiskey lover there for it; whether one may be sent to a table is a question for the manager.

producer.sayIt: Dareringer is a Louisville bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks, rich with dried fruit under the Birdcage's smoke.
askKitchen: How is the Birdcage smoked, and with what wood?
