producer.history:
Tullamore D.E.W. traces its start to 1829, when Michael Molloy founded a distillery at Tullamore in County Offaly, a site most likely chosen for the Grand Canal beside it. After Molloy's death in 1857 it passed in time to his nephew, Bernard Daly.

The letters belong to Daniel E. Williams, who lived from 1848 to 1921; most sources give his middle name as Edmund. By the brand's account he started at the distillery as a stable boy at 15, and he rose to run it as general manager and later came to own it. By one account he added his initials to the whiskey's name in 1887, and they spell dew as well.

The old distillery closed in the 1950s and the brand name was sold in 1965; for decades the whiskey was made at Midleton. In 2010 the Scottish firm William Grant & Sons bought Tullamore D.E.W., and on 17 September 2014 it opened a new distillery at Clonminch, just outside the town, the first new Irish distillery on a greenfield site in over a century.

The whiskey is triple distilled and blended from the three Irish styles: pot still, malt and grain. The result is light and smooth, which suits hot coffee and cream.
facts: Founded in 1829 at Tullamore, County Offaly, by Michael Molloy, beside the Grand Canal.
D.E.W. are the initials of Daniel E. Williams, 1848 to 1921, general manager and later owner; by the brand's account he started as a stable boy.
By one account Williams added his initials to the brand name in 1887.
The original distillery closed in the 1950s and the brand name was sold in 1965.
William Grant & Sons bought the brand in 2010 and opened a new distillery at Clonminch on 17 September 2014.
Triple distilled and blended from pot still, malt and grain whiskey.
The Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco, where Irish coffee was recreated in 1952, has poured Tullamore D.E.W. since 2006.
notes: The menu prints Tullamore Dew; the bottle writes D.E.W. When a guest asks, the letters are the initials of Daniel E. Williams, who by the brand's account rose from stable boy to owner.
Sources spell his middle name Edmund, Edmond or Edward; Daniel E. Williams is the careful form to say aloud.
Do not say it has been made in Tullamore without a break since 1829: the old distillery closed in the 1950s and the new one opened in 2014.
It is owned by William Grant & Sons, the Scottish firm; name nobody from the company.
A good link to tell: the Buena Vista in San Francisco, which made Irish coffee famous in America, has poured Tullamore since 2006.
producer.sayIt: Tullamore D.E.W. is a triple distilled Irish whiskey from County Offaly; the letters are the initials of Daniel E. Williams.
askKitchen: Which Tullamore D.E.W. bottling goes into Brennan's Irish Coffee?

producer.history:
Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is the work of Jade Liqueurs, a company founded in 2000 by a New Orleans-born scientist and absinthe historian. He researched surviving pre-ban absinthes and the old methods of making them, aiming to recreate the spirit as it was before the bans of the early twentieth century, without the myths that had grown up around it. Nouvelle-Orléans was the first Jade absinthe; a specialist retailer dates it to 2004 and says the founder has personally produced every batch since.

It is made at the Combier distillery in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, chosen partly for its historic equipment: copper bain-marie alembics built in the 1870s and acquired from one of the original absinthe distilleries of Pontarlier, France. Wormwood and other plants are macerated in wine alcohol and distilled, and a second infusion of plants in the distillate gives the pale green colour. It is bottled at 68 percent.

The name is a tribute to the founder's home city and its nineteenth-century absinthe culture. Its sellers describe the style as rooted in the absinthes that made the Sazerac and the Absinthe Frappé famous: fresh, with a peppery spice.

At Brennan's it is printed only on the Origin Story, the top of the Sazerac ladder, beside Dudognon Cognac and barrel-aged Peychaud's.

notes: Say it as a French absinthe made as a New Orleans tribute: distilled in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, not in the city.
Name no one behind it: say the founder, a New Orleans-born scientist who researched the absinthes made before the ban.
Guests ask whether absinthe makes you see things. The honest answer: wormwood does not cause hallucinations, and absinthe has been sold legally in the United States again since 2007.
At 68 percent it is strong, but it perfumes the Origin Story; describe the aroma, floral wormwood and fennel, not the strength.
Whether the bar rinses the glass with it, as the Classic is rinsed with Herbsaint, is a lineup question; do not describe the build until it is confirmed.
producer.sayIt: Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is a French absinthe, distilled in Saumur as a tribute to New Orleans' nineteenth-century absinthe culture.
askKitchen: Is the Origin Story's glass rinsed with the Jade, as the Classic is with Herbsaint, or is the Jade added another way?

producer.history:
St. George Spirits was founded in 1982 as an eau de vie distillery, making clear fruit brandies. Its founder was master distiller for 28 years before handing the role to his successor in 2010. In 2004 the company moved into a 65,000-square-foot aircraft hangar on the former Alameda Naval Air Station, where it still distils.

When absinthe returned to American shelves in 2007, once federal regulators accepted that a properly made one met the thujone limit, St. George had a recipe ready, developed over eleven years. The label office refused the label several times, objecting to the monkey on it and to the word Verte, before approving it in early December 2007. St. George Absinthe Verte went on sale on 21 December 2007, the first legal American-made absinthe in 95 years, and the first 1,800 bottles sold out in six hours.

It is built on brandy rather than the beet spirit of many absinthes. Wormwood, fennel and star anise are infused in the brandy and distilled; the distillate is then infused with mint, tarragon, Genovese basil, lemon balm, hyssop and stinging nettle, which give the green colour and a garden character. Star anise is itself a departure from the green anise of the classic European recipes. It is bottled at 60 percent.

At Brennan's it rinses the glass of Thompson's Dream, the first step up from the Classic Sazerac, in place of the Classic's Herbsaint.

producer.history:
The Bitter Truth was founded in Munich in 2006 by two working bartenders. Their first releases came out in August 2006, an Orange Bitters and an Old Time Aromatic Bitters, and the company grew into an award-winning range that includes recreations of historical styles, such as Jerry Thomas' Own Decanter Bitters, a blend of citrus, dried fruit, cloves, angostura bark and cinnamon.

Creole Bitters were new by 2010, when a review called them the newest in the range. They are made in the New Orleans style: bright red, led by anise and caraway, with fennel, cinnamon and a little pepper behind and a floral finish. They are sold at 39 percent alcohol.

The name says what they are and what they are not. Peychaud's, the red bitters of the Classic Sazerac, is a Sazerac Company brand; The Bitter Truth sells its New Orleans-style bitters as Creole Bitters. Retailers sell The Bitter Truth's as a natural substitute in a Sazerac, and one reviewer found them very similar to Peychaud's and arguably more aromatic.

At Brennan's they are printed only in Thompson's Dream, with Willett 4-year rye and the St. George absinthe rinse, where they take the place of the Classic's Peychaud's.

Its first releases, in August 2006, were Orange Bitters and Old Time Aromatic Bitters.
Creole Bitters were the newest in the range in a 2010 review: New Orleans-inspired, anise and caraway, a floral finish.
Retailers also list fennel, cinnamon, cayenne and pink peppercorn; the bitters are bright red and 39 percent alcohol.
Sold as a natural substitute for Peychaud's in a Sazerac; one reviewer found them arguably more aromatic.
Peychaud's is a Sazerac Company brand name; The Bitter Truth sells its New Orleans-style bitters as Creole Bitters.
The range includes Jerry Thomas' Own Decanter Bitters, with citrus, dried fruit, cloves, angostura bark and cinnamon.

Guests ask why German bitters go into a New Orleans drink. The honest answer: they are made in the New Orleans style and sold for exactly this drink, the Sazerac.

producer.sayIt: Bitter Truth Creole Bitters come from Munich: a red, anise-led tribute to the New Orleans style, in place of Peychaud's.

producer.where: Trinidad; begun in Angostura, Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar
producer.history:
Angostura bitters began with Dr Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German surgeon born in 1796 who served in Simón Bolívar's army and settled around 1820 in the town of Angostura, Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar. The company says he had perfected his Amargo Aromatico by 1824, as a medicine for soldiers; Wikipedia, citing an 1876 court case, says he began selling it that year and set up a distillery in 1830. The bitters took the town's name.

Dr Siegert died in 1870, according to Difford's Guide, and in 1875 the family business, J.G.B. Siegert & Hijos, moved to Port of Spain, Trinidad, amid unrest in Venezuela. It has stayed on the island, adding rum from 1947 through Trinidad Distillers Limited. In 1982 it was listed on the Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange as Angostura Holdings. Reports in 2025 named its largest shareholder as Rumpro, part of the CL Financial group, which has been in liquidation since 2017, with the government's National Investment Fund Holding Company second. The bitters marked their bicentennial in 2024.

The recipe is a trade secret, and the label names only gentian among the botanicals. The oversized label has a legend of its own, most often told as a mix-up between the founder's sons over the bottle and the label that was never corrected. The label still shows a medal from the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.

At Brennan's it seasons the Birdcage, a smoked Old Fashioned, and the menu prints it with a demerara sugar cube in the Champagne Cocktail.
facts: Created by Dr Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, born in 1796, a German surgeon in Simón Bolívar's army, at Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar.
The company dates his formula, Amargo Aromatico, to 1824, made as a medicine for soldiers.
In 1875 the business, J.G.B. Siegert & Hijos, moved to Port of Spain, Trinidad.
The label names one botanical, gentian; the full recipe is a trade secret.
Stories differ on why the label is oversized; the usual one is a mix-up between the founder's sons over bottle and label, never corrected.
The label shows a medal from the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.
Rum came later, from 1947, through Trinidad Distillers Limited.
Listed in 1982 as Angostura Holdings; reports in 2025 named Rumpro, of the CL Financial group, the largest shareholder and the government's National Investment Fund second.
The bitters marked their bicentennial in 2024.
notes: Never confuse it with Peychaud's: Angostura, dark and clove-spiced, is in the Birdcage and the Champagne Cocktail; Peychaud's, red and anise-led, is the Sazerac's.
Guests ask whether it holds angostura bark. The honest answer: the bitters are named for the town, not the bark; published histories say the bark is not in them, and the recipe is secret.
The Champagne Cocktail prints Angostura with a demerara sugar cube; in the classic build the bitters soak the cube, which keeps bubbles rising. Confirm the house build at lineup.
The bitters are named for a town in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar, and are made in Trinidad today.
The Birdcage's measure and how it is smoked are the bar's to confirm; say Angostura seasons it, nothing more.
producer.sayIt: Angostura is the classic aromatic bitters, made in Trinidad to a secret recipe begun in Venezuela in 1824.
askKitchen: Is the Champagne Cocktail's sugar cube soaked with Angostura before the Champagne goes in, and with how many dashes?

producer.history:
The Dudognon family has grown vines at Lignières-Sonneville, in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first cru, since 1776; one history says the present estate was bought in 1852. The vineyard, Le Davore, lies on a chalky hillside tucked away from the village. Paulin Dudognon brought the house its first formal recognition, a gold medal in 1898.

For generations the family supplied its eaux-de-vie to the large Cognac houses. Raymond Dudognon, born in 1927 into a line of distillers going back to Paulin, took over in 1946 and was the first to sell cognac under the family name; one account dates that change to 1970. Raymond died in 2002, having chosen one of his three daughters to succeed him. She runs the house with her husband and their son, and every source found still names the family as its owners.

It is a bouilleur de cru, a grower that distils only its own grapes. The family distils over a wood fire on two copper alembic stills, roughly 100 barrels a year, air-dries the oak for its casks for five years, and adds nothing to the cognac but water. The cognacs are sold by age: a 10-year bottling, a 15-year Napoléon, the 20-year Vieille Réserve and a 60-year cognac named for Paulin.

At Brennan's the Origin Story prints Dudognon Cognac without naming the bottling, so which one the bar pours is a lineup question.

producer.history:
Daron is a Calvados Pays d'Auge from Maison Ferrand, a house from Cognac. Difford's Guide lists Ferrand as both producer and owner, and retailers describe the calvados as made under Ferrand's direction, bringing a Cognac house's distilling experience to the orchards of Normandy's Pays d'Auge. It is not a Christian Drouin calvados: Drouin is a separate family house in the same appellation. No public source found here names the Normandy distillery or the year the brand began.

Calvados is apple brandy from Normandy: cider, sometimes with some pear, distilled and aged in oak. Pays d'Auge is its most exacting appellation, which requires double distillation in copper pot stills. Daron's cider comes from Normandy cider apples, Bisquets, Bedan, Petit Joly and St Martin, with a little pear, distilled slowly in copper pot stills and aged in Limousin oak.

Fine is the entry-level bottling of the Daron range. Difford's gives it no age statement but says it is aged an average of five years in small oak casks, in warehouses with traditional earth floors. Tasting notes speak of baked apple, honey and warm spice, ginger and clove, with a fairly dry finish.

At Brennan's it is the base of To Each His Own, with Lillet Blanc and quince liqueur, a drink named for the 1946 song.

producer.sayIt: Daron Fine is Calvados from Normandy's Pays d'Auge, apple brandy double distilled in copper pot stills, from the Cognac house Maison Ferrand.

producer.who: Chartreuse, made by the Carthusian monks
producer.where: Aiguenoire distillery, near Voiron, in the French Alps
producer.founded: Manuscript 1605; Elixir 1737; Green Chartreuse 1764 by most accounts
producer.history:
Chartreuse is made by the Carthusians, the order of the Grande Chartreuse monastery in the French Alps. By the order's story, in 1605 the Maréchal d'Estrées, a marshal of Henry IV's artillery, gave the monks a manuscript recipe for an elixir of 130 plants. It was so hard to decipher that only by 1737 had the monastery's apothecary, Brother Jérôme Maubec, worked out a practical recipe for the Elixir. Most accounts date Green Chartreuse, a milder liqueur adapted from it, to 1764, though sources differ on who finished the work. It is bottled at 55 percent.

The monks have been driven out more than once. Expelled from France in 1903, they made their liqueur in Tarragona, in Spain, while the French state sold the Chartreuse name to a commercial company; in 1929 they were allowed to use the name again, and Tarragona kept distilling until 1989. Production later settled in Voiron and, since 2018, at a new distillery at Aiguenoire.

Only the monks know the full recipe. The dried plants are sorted, crushed and mixed at the monastery, then sent to the distillery. In 2021 the monks decided not to raise output, and a letter of January 2023 explained why: their life of solitude and prayer comes first. Output was held at about 1.6 million bottles a year, and every market went on allocation.

At Brennan's it is the herbal heart of Five Minutes More.

At 55 percent it is strong and a little carries a drink; how much goes into Five Minutes More is the bar's to say.
If asked about the green, say the colour is natural, from the plants; never say it is dyed.
Yellow Chartreuse is the gentler, sweeter sister; the menu prints the Green.

producer.history:
Licor 43, Cuarenta y Tres in Spanish, comes from Cartagena, in Spain. The brand tells a story of Carthago Nova, the ancient city there, where in 209 BC the Romans are said to have found a golden liqueur, liqvor mirabilis. That is the brand's legend, not history, but it is the idea the recipe is said to build on.

Commercial production began in 1946 in a small distillery in Cartagena, with the liqueur bottled by hand. The recipe is credited to three siblings of the founding family and a brother-in-law, and it is still a closely guarded secret: by one account only the family and the factory's director know it in full. The name is the number of ingredients, 43, and only a handful have been made public: vanilla, orange peel, lemon, coriander and tea.

It is often called the most popular liqueur in Spain. The brand belongs to Zamora Company, and its factory, just outside Cartagena, makes it from start to finish and houses a museum open for tours. It is bottled at 31 percent.

At Brennan's it rounds off Five Minutes More, with Green Chartreuse, Cathead mandarin vodka and lemon. The founding year is also the year Brennan's opened: a happy coincidence, never a connection.

Bottled at 31 percent alcohol.

producer.sayIt: Licor 43 is a golden Spanish liqueur from Cartagena, made since 1946 from 43 ingredients, led by vanilla and citrus.

producer.history:
Lillet was founded in 1872 in Podensac, south of Bordeaux, by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet, wine and spirits merchants who took up distilling. Their early trade was mainly in fruit liqueurs. Their first wine aperitif came in 1887: Kina Lillet, its name joining the family's to quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine.

The recipe is still about 85 percent wine and 15 percent fruit liqueurs and cinchona. For the Blanc the wine is Semillon, with some Sauvignon Blanc, and the liqueurs are made by steeping the peels of sweet oranges, from Morocco or Spain, and bitter oranges, from Haiti or Peru, in alcohol for several weeks. The blend is matured in oak casks in the Podensac cellars and bottled at 17 percent.

In 1986 Lillet Blanc replaced Kina Lillet: sweeter and less bitter. That is why a Vesper made today does not taste as it did when it was written. The family sold the business in 1985, and in 2008 it passed to a subsidiary of Pernod Ricard, which owns it today.

At Brennan's it appears twice: topped with sparkling wine and lemon in the Riviera, and beside Daron Calvados and quince liqueur in To Each His Own.

producer.who: L.N. Mattei, makers of Cap Corse Mattei
producer.history:
Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his first shop in Bastia, on Corsica, in 1872, selling cigars, coffee, wine and liqueurs. In 1874 he began distilling cédrat, the thick-skinned citron of Cap Corse, the island's northern peninsula, and in 1875 he made a medicinal wine with quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine. Accounts differ on how he came to the bark: his importer says he found it on a voyage to the Caribbean; another source says he meant it against malaria.

The Blanc is a mistelle: Muscat and Vermentinu grape must kept from fermenting with neutral alcohol, so its sweetness is the grape's own. It is flavoured with cinchona, cédrat and other plants, fruits and spices, and bottled at 17 percent. The bark brings spice and gentle bitterness to the middle and finish; the cédrat brings citrus perfume and a silky texture.

Its American importer has long called the house family owned, with macerations, ageing and bottling done in house, by one report in the Borgo industrial zone. Monocle reports, though, that a Corsican drinks group, Groupe Boisson Corse, has since bought the house, revived the founder's recipe and taken output from about 80,000 bottles to about 400,000. On Cap Corse stands the Moulin Mattei, a windmill a later head of the house turned into an advertisement for the aperitif; the Conservatoire du Littoral bought it in 2004 and restored its 1930s look.

At Brennan's it plays the vermouth's part in the Spoonbill, with Hendrick's gin and chive oil.

askKitchen: Is the Spoonbill stirred like a martini, and in what proportion of gin to Cap Corse?

producer.history:
Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which grows wild in southern Africa. The first product was a clear marula spirit, bottled in 1983. Cream was added to the recipe and the cream liqueur reached shelves in 1989, first marketed that September by the Southern Liqueur Company, part of Distell. In 2023 Heineken Beverages acquired Distell, and with it the brand.

The harvest runs from about mid-January to March around Phalaborwa. The ripe fruit falls and is gathered by women from the local rural communities, then taken to Amarula's plant in Phalaborwa, where the flesh is separated from the hard stones. The pulp is kept cool so it cannot ferment on its own and goes to the cellars in Stellenbosch, where it is fermented much like wine. It is distilled twice, first in column stills, then in copper pot stills, aged two years in small oak barrels and blended with fresh cream. It is bottled at 17 percent.

Elephants love marula fruit, which is why one is on the label. The story that elephants get drunk on fallen fruit was challenged by a 2006 study, and scientists still argue about it.

At Brennan's it is the South Africa in Floating in South Africa, with housemade vanilla bean ice cream and Abita root beer.

producer.sayIt: Amarula is a South African cream liqueur made from the wild marula fruit, distilled, aged two years in oak and blended with cream.
askKitchen: Is Floating in South Africa built as a float, the Amarula over the ice cream before the root beer, or blended?

producer.history:
Frangelico is a hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, launched in 1978 by the Barbero family company, founded in 1891, and made in Canale, in the heart of the region's hazelnut country. Its name and look come from a legend: a hermit monk called Fra Angelico, said to have lived in the Piedmont hills. The older brand story placed him in the seventeenth century and never claimed he made liqueur, so it is told as legend. The bottle is shaped like a friar's habit, with a knotted cord that was tied by hand until 2003.

It is made from Tonda Gentile hazelnuts from the Langhe, a variety with protected status; the brand buys about 38 tons a year. The nuts are shelled, toasted and crushed, infused in alcohol and water, and distilled. The hazelnut distillate is blended with cocoa, vanilla and roasted coffee, rested, and bottled at 20 percent.

In 2010 William Grant & Sons bought Frangelico in a package with Tullamore Dew, then sold it later that year, with Carolans and Irish Mist, to Gruppo Campari, already the liqueur's global source. At the time the United States was its largest market, about half of sales.

At Brennan's it is in two coffee cocktails: the Espresso Martini, with Kahlua, and Ralph’s Coffee, with Nocello.

producer.history:
Kahlúa is a coffee liqueur first produced in Veracruz, Mexico, in 1936; Wikipedia credits the Pedro Domecq company with beginning its production. The name is usually explained as Veracruz Nahuatl for House of the Acolhua people; the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails derives it instead from kahwa, the Arabic word for coffee. Neither is settled.

It was almost unknown until the early 1960s, when an American importer took the United States rights and promoted it hard, and sales took off. The Domecq business became part of Allied Domecq in 1994, and in 2005 Pernod Ricard acquired the brand, which it still owns.

It is made by blending roasted, ground arabica coffee with water and sugar cane spirit, adding vanilla and caramel, and resting the blend before bottling. The coffee and the cane are grown in Veracruz; sources disagree on where the blending is done, and Difford's Guide and the Oxford Companion place it in Mexico City. Long bottled at 26.5 percent, it was cut to 20 percent in 2003 or 2004, by differing accounts, and to 16 percent in some markets in 2021.

At Brennan's it is in the Espresso Martini, with chicory, vodka and Frangelico; the menu spells it Kahlua.

producer.sayIt: Kahlúa is Mexico's coffee liqueur, made since 1936 from Veracruz arabica, sugar cane spirit, vanilla and caramel.

producer.where: Savignano sul Panaro, near Modena, Emilia-Romagna, Italy
producer.history:
Nocello is made by Toschi, a family company founded in 1945 in Vignola, near Modena, by two brothers. They began by preserving cherries in spirit, and the company still specialises in fruit in spirit, liqueurs and products for gelato. Its working headquarters are now at Savignano sul Panaro, close by.

Nocello is made from walnuts and hazelnuts. It is amber, sweet and rounded, with a balanced walnut flavour and tones of vanilla, and bottled at 24 percent; in 2004 it won a gold medal at the IWSC. In the United States its label reads Imitation Liqueur. Toschi has not published its method, so a server describes the taste, not a process.

It belongs to the walnut liqueur tradition of Emilia-Romagna, whose best-known member is nocino, the dark liqueur made by steeping green walnuts in alcohol; by custom the walnuts are picked around St John's Day, 24 June. Toschi makes a Nocino too. Nocello is the lighter, sweeter cousin.

At Brennan's it goes into Ralph’s Coffee, with dark roast coffee and chicory, Frangelico and whipped cream: a roasty, nutty after-dinner coffee.

producer.who: Pedro Ximénez, the sweet sherry style (bodega not printed)
producer.where: Jerez, Spain, with most PX grapes grown in Montilla-Moriles
producer.history:
Pedro Ximénez, PX for short, is both a white grape and the sweetest, darkest style of sherry. The grapes are left on the vine until very ripe, picked by hand and laid on straw mats to dry in the sun, a practice called asoleo. They shrink towards raisins, losing water and concentrating sugar, so the must is so dense that fermentation often stalls. The wine is fortified and aged until it is almost black and syrupy, tasting of raisin, fig and molasses.

Most PX grapes grow not in Jerez but in Montilla-Moriles. Jerez bodegas often buy PX must or wine from there and age and blend it in their own cellars, where it must rest at least two years before it may be called sherry. The Jerez rules allow PX only for sweet wines, and it also sweetens other sherries into cream styles.

Sherry itself, its towns, its solera and its denomination of 1933, has its own profile with the aged sherry of the Turtle Soup, so this one keeps to PX.

At Brennan's it gives Banane au Chocolat its dried fruit depth, under crème de banane and crème de cacao. The menu names no bodega. Casks that once held PX also finish the Rabbit Hole bourbon in the Birdcage.

Guests may have heard the grape came to Spain from Germany with a soldier. The honest answer: it is an old story, and no source found here supports it.
A link across the list: the Rabbit Hole Dareringer in the Birdcage is finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks.
producer.sayIt: Pedro Ximénez is Spain's sweetest sherry, made from sun-dried grapes: dark, syrupy, tasting of raisin and fig.
askKitchen: Which Pedro Ximénez sherry, from which bodega, goes into Banane au Chocolat?

producer.who: Pimento dram, the allspice liqueur of Jamaica
producer.founded: An article of commerce since the 1850s
producer.history:
Allspice dram, called pimento dram in Jamaica, is rum in which allspice berries have been steeped, then sweetened. Allspice is the dried berry of the pimento tree; the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails says its flavour recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, and records the dram as an article of commerce since the 1850s. Bottles were shown at the International Exhibition of 1862. In Jamaica the berry kept its Spanish name, pimiento, now pimento; the English called it allspice. It is no relation of the pimento pepper.

The National Museum Jamaica records that the liqueur became popular in Europe and North America in the early 1900s, when J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it. It appeared in drinks such as the Lion's Tail and was taken up by the tiki bars. Imports to the United States later stopped, and bartenders made their own.

The revival came in 2008 with St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria from Jamaican allspice berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled Jamaican rum for an American importer.

At Brennan's it gives For Sentimental Reasons its warm baking spice, under pear purée and sparkling wine. The menu names no brand, so which dram the bar pours is a lineup question.
facts: Allspice dram is rum steeped with allspice berries and sweetened, a Jamaican liqueur.
Its flavour recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, says the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails.
An article of commerce since the 1850s; shown at the International Exhibition of 1862.
J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it in the early 1900s, by the National Museum Jamaica's record.
In Jamaica the berry is called pimento, from the Spanish; it is no relation of the pimento pepper.
St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria with Jamaican berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled rum, debuted in 2008.
notes: Say it as Jamaica's spiced rum liqueur: clove, cinnamon and nutmeg in one berry.
The menu names no brand; describe the flavour and let the bar name the bottle.
It is sweet spice, not heat: never call it pepper or say the drink is hot.
A little carries the drink: For Sentimental Reasons is pear and bubbles first, with the spice underneath.
producer.sayIt: Allspice dram is Jamaica's pimento dram: rum steeped with allspice berries, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once.
askKitchen: Which allspice dram goes into For Sentimental Reasons: St. Elizabeth, another brand, or a house infusion?

producer.where: Krzesk, near Siedlce, east of Warsaw, Poland
producer.history:
Chopin is a Polish vodka named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favoured son of Poland. It is made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, east of Warsaw, at a distillery near the hamlet of Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896. The brand says its still of that year is one of the oldest remaining stills in Poland.

The brand dates from the early 1990s: sources give 1992 or 1993. When its founder bought the distillery itself is less clear: one account says 1993, another 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997. The company calls itself family owned and run, now in its second generation, and Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.

Chopin is a single-ingredient vodka. Each bottling is made from one raw material, potato, rye or wheat, and distilled four times. The brand grows some of its ingredients on its own farmland and buys the rest from family farms near the distillery, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds. The potato vodka, the best known bottling, uses Stobrawa potatoes, which retailers say are grown in Podlasie.

Potato vodka is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness. Which Chopin goes into the Flamingo is a question for the bar.
facts: Named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favoured son of Poland.
Made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, at a distillery near Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896.
A single-ingredient vodka: each bottling is made from potato, rye or wheat alone and distilled four times.
The brand dates from 1992 or 1993 by different sources; the distillery purchase is dated 1993 or 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997.
The brand says its ingredients grow on its own land or on nearby family farms, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds.
The potato vodka uses Stobrawa potatoes, grown in Podlasie by retailers’ accounts.
Family owned and run, in its second generation; the company calls itself Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.

Guests ask whether potato vodka tastes of potato. The honest answer: hardly; it is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness.

producer.sayIt: Chopin is a Polish single-ingredient vodka, distilled four times at a family-owned distillery that has made vodka since 1896.

producer.where: Near Loßburg, in the Black Forest, Germany
producer.history:
Monkey 47 tells its own story through a British officer. By the brand’s account, Montgomery Collins, known as Monty, a Royal Air Force officer posted to Berlin after the Second World War, sponsored a monkey named Max at the Berlin Zoo. He left the air force in 1951, settled in the northern Black Forest and opened a guesthouse, Zum Wilden Affen, the Wild Monkey, where his Schwarzwald Dry Gin was the house drink until the 1970s. No archive or independent account of him has been found, so it is told as the brand’s story.

The modern gin began in 2008, when the founder, from a German brandy family, left a job at Nokia to recreate the recipe in the Black Forest. After more than 120 trial distillations the gin came to market, usually dated 2010. In January 2016 Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed to buy a majority stake, and in March 2020 Pernod Ricard bought the rest, with the founder staying on as an adviser. The distillery near Loßburg, built in 2015, centres on a custom still from a German coppersmith.

The name holds the numbers: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. About a third of the botanicals are Black Forest plants, among them spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves, and the citrus peels go in fresh. They macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water before distillation in small stills; the gin then rests in large earthenware vessels for about three months, is cut slowly with water and is bottled without chill filtration.
facts: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol give the gin its name; about a third of the botanicals come from the Black Forest.
Black Forest botanicals include spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves; the citrus peels are used fresh.
Botanicals macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water, about 36 hours by one account, before distillation in small stills.
The gin rests in large earthenware vessels, 90 or 100 days by different accounts, before slow dilution; it is not chill filtered.
By the brand’s account, the RAF officer Montgomery Collins opened the Zum Wilden Affen guesthouse in the Black Forest after leaving the air force in 1951.
The founder began recreating the recipe in 2008, over more than 120 trial distillations; the launch is usually dated 2010.
Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed a majority stake in January 2016, and Pernod Ricard bought the rest in March 2020; neither price was disclosed.
The distillery near Loßburg was built in 2015 around a custom still made by a German coppersmith.
notes: Tell the Montgomery Collins story as the brand’s story: no archive or independent account confirming the officer, the guesthouse or the recipe was found.
Guests ask about the 47: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. It is a strong, aromatic gin, which is why it still reads under the Champagne in the Flamingo.
The menu prints Monkey 47 Schwarzwald Gin; the bottle says Schwarzwald Dry Gin. Schwarzwald is German for the Black Forest.
If asked who owns it: Pernod Ricard, the sole owner since 2020 after buying a majority in 2016. Name nobody; the founder is said as the founder.
Do not call it a British gin: it is German, made in the Black Forest.
producer.sayIt: Monkey 47 is a Black Forest gin: 47 botanicals at 47 percent, a third of them from the forest, rested in earthenware before bottling.

producer.history:
Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin made by William Grant & Sons, the family-owned company William Grant founded in 1887, the year his Glenfiddich distillery began production, and still run by his descendants. The gin is made at Girvan, where the company built its grain distillery in 1963 under a great-grandson of William Grant.

That same great-grandson bought two old stills at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still built in 1948 by John Dore & Co. By the company’s account, in 1988 he set a company distiller the task of making one spirit from both. After years of trials Hendrick’s launched in 1999: the gins of the two stills are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added. Because the rose and cucumber go in after distillation, it cannot be labelled a London Dry gin.

Eleven botanicals stand behind the rose and cucumber, among them juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow, caraway and lemon and orange peel. The rose is described as Bulgarian; the cucumbers come from Holland or Belgium. The name, by most accounts, was chosen by a member of the Grant family after Hendrick, a gardener who took particular care of the family’s roses.

On 1 October 2018 the company opened the Hendrick’s Gin Palace in the grounds at Girvan, with new still houses that doubled capacity and glasshouses of exotic botanicals.

Two stills bought at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still of 1948.
Launched in 1999: the two stills’ spirits are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added.
Because rose and cucumber go in after distillation, Hendrick’s cannot be labelled a London Dry gin.
Eleven botanicals besides rose and cucumber, including juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow and caraway.

notes: Say Hendrick’s is Scottish, made at Girvan by William Grant & Sons, the family company behind Glenfiddich.
Guests ask why it is not a London Dry: the rose and cucumber are added after distillation, which a London Dry may not do.
Name nobody from the company: say a great-grandson of William Grant, or the master distiller.
The still dates vary by source; if asked, quote the company’s own: the Bennett of 1860 and the Carter-Head of 1948.
In the Spoonbill the cucumber meets the chive oil and the rose meets the Cap Corse quinquina: say cool, green and floral.
producer.sayIt: Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin from Girvan, made in two old stills and finished with rose and cucumber; it launched in 1999.

producer.who: Gentilly Gin, Seven Three Distilling Co.
producer.where: 301 North Claiborne Avenue, Tremé, New Orleans
producer.history:
Seven Three Distilling Co. is a New Orleans craft distillery named for the city’s 73 officially recognised neighbourhoods, and it names its spirits after them: St. Roch Vodka, Bywater Bourbon, Marigny Moonshine, Irish Channel Whiskey, Black Pearl Rum and Gentilly Gin. A New Orleans husband and wife developed the brand while building a custom distillery, which opened in early 2017 in a warehouse at 301 North Claiborne Avenue, on the corner of Bienville Street, usually described as Tremé. Its first release was a run of 1,000 bottles of St. Roch Vodka, a neutral spirit redistilled and filtered for five days through copper, limestone and charcoal.

Gentilly Gin starts from the same neutral base. Juniper is joined by persimmon and elderflower, 17 botanicals in all, inspired by the traiteurs, the old faith healers of Louisiana. It is bottled at 87 proof, 43.5 percent. Tasters find elderflower, a little anise and vanilla on the nose, honeyed persimmon, ginger and juniper on the palate, and a peppery finish. A Barrel Reserve version rests in barrels before bottling.

Gentilly itself is one of the city’s old neighbourhoods. By the common account, in 1727 the colonists Mathurin and Pierre Dreux chose the natural levee along Bayou Sauvage for their plantation and named it after the French community they came from; one recent history argues the name began as Chantilly.

producer.history:
Cathead Distillery was founded in 2010 by two friends and blues fans who had spent about eleven years working in South Carolina before coming home to Jackson, Mississippi. Mississippi passed statewide prohibition in 1907 and was the last state to repeal it, in 1966, and then only county by county; the founders had to help amend several old state laws before they could open. Cathead went to market in May 2010, and Visit Jackson and the company’s own releases call it Mississippi’s first legal distillery.

It began in Gluckstadt and moved downtown to 422 South Farish Street in 2015. The name is blues slang: the old blues players called each other cats, as a term of respect. The logo draws on the folk art of the Delta bluesman James Son Thomas, who sculpted cat heads from river clay, and the company has sent part of its sales to music nonprofits.

Cathead makes vodkas, Bristow Gin, a chicory liqueur called Hoodoo and Old Soul Bourbon in small batches. Its vodka is made in runs of 500 gallons or less, with some sweet corn in the grain for a crisp finish, and bottled at 80 proof. Beside the plain vodka come flavoured ones: honeysuckle, pecan, a bitter orange made with bitter orange and satsuma extracts, and a Satsuma Mandarin Vodka listed on the distillery’s shop pages, most likely the bottle the menu calls Cathead Mandarin Vodka. No source gives its proof or how it is flavoured; a canned Satsuma Mandarin vodka soda at 5 percent is a different product.

Visit Jackson and the company’s releases call it Mississippi’s first legal distillery.

producer.who: Volcán De Mi Tierra, Moët Hennessy
producer.where: Distillery NOM 1523, at the foot of the Tequila Volcano, Jalisco, Mexico
producer.history:
Volcán De Mi Tierra, the volcano of my land, is a tequila house born of a partnership between Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, and a Mexican family whose lineage in Mexico goes back to the seventeenth century. By the brand’s story, a meeting between a family elder and LVMH executives raised the question of why the group had no tequila. The family owned land and a small distillery near the long-dormant Tequila Volcano in Jalisco; the partners chose the distillery, NOM 1523, revamped it and revived a brand the family had called Volcán. It has been described as the first 50:50 partnership LVMH had entered.

The tequila launched on 1 May 2017 with a Blanco and a Cristalino, a blend of añejo and extra añejo tequilas filtered clear, in eight American cities and Mexico. In October 2025 it was named the Official Tequila of Formula 1 under LVMH’s ten-year deal with the series.

The brand says the volcano’s ash left a soil rich in basalt and iron, which gives the tequila its taste. The agave comes from two terroirs: the highlands, at about 1,700 metres on iron-rich red clay, and the lowlands, at about 1,000 metres on dark volcanic soil that gives earthier, spicier notes. The Reposado rests in American and European oak, 135 days by one account and nine months by another, and is bottled at 40 percent: honey, dried fruit, toasted nuts, oak and vanilla.

producer.founded: 1734, as a Champagne trading house; the Taittinger family bought it in 1932
producer.history:
Taittinger traces its start to 1734, when Jacques Fourneaux began trading Champagne wines and worked with the Benedictine abbeys that owned some of the best vineyards. In the 1820s the firm became Forest-Fourneaux, and in 1932 Pierre Taittinger bought it and gave it his name; one source gives 1931.

In the years from 1945 to 1960 the house set up its cellars in the Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath the site of the Saint-Nicaise abbey in Reims, where the wines still age. In 2005 the family sold its group to the American fund Starwood Capital Group; in 2006 a family-led bid, backed by the bank Crédit Agricole, bought the Champagne house back. A member of the family has been president since 1 January 2020.

Brut La Française is the house’s non-vintage Brut. Its mark is a high share of Chardonnay for a non-vintage blend, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Meunier, which gives the light, fresh, elegant style the house is known for. One reviewer says it spends a year longer on its lees than the Brut Réserve, which ages at least three years.

At Brennan’s it tops the Flamingo in the Roost, and the same wine sits on the Birthday Bubbles list as a 3 litre double magnum.

producer.sayIt: The Flamingo is topped with Taittinger La Française, a Chardonnay-led Champagne from a Reims house whose story begins in 1734.

producer.who: Chandon, the sparkling wine house of Moët Hennessy (LVMH)
producer.where: Yountville, Napa Valley, California; the Garden Spritz is made in Mendoza, Argentina
producer.history:
Chandon is the sparkling wine house the Moët group built beyond Champagne. Its first venture abroad was Chandon Argentina, founded by Moët & Chandon in 1959 at Agrelo, in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza: the first Moët & Chandon subsidiary outside France.

In California it began in 1973, first named M & H Vineyards after its parent, Moët Hennessy. Its founding head, John Wright, found the vineyards; the first vintages were made at the Trefethen winery, and the house moved into its own winery at Yountville in 1977. Wine Spectator calls it the first French sparkling wine house in California. LVMH owns it today.

Chandon Brut is a dry, non-vintage sparkling wine made by the traditional method, its second fermentation in the bottle, with Chardonnay from southern Napa, Mt. Veeder and Carneros in the blend: green apple, pear, citrus and a little brioche.

The Garden Spritz is Argentine. Chandon’s winemakers in Mendoza made a bitter orange Garden liqueur from Valencia oranges, herbs and spices, inspired by Argentina’s taste for yerba maté and Fernet, and blended it with the Chandon Brut made in Mendoza. Chandon announced it in the United States in May 2021 as its first ready-to-drink sparkling aperitif.
facts: Chandon Argentina, founded by Moët & Chandon in 1959 at Agrelo in Mendoza, was the first Moët & Chandon subsidiary outside France.
Chandon California was founded in 1973 by Moët Hennessy, first named M & H Vineyards after its parent company.
Wine Spectator calls it the first French sparkling wine house in California, making wine by the Champagne method.
Its first vintages were made at the Trefethen winery; it moved into its own winery at Yountville in 1977.
Owned today by LVMH, Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy.
Chandon Brut is dry and non-vintage, made by the traditional method; sources disagree on its grape split, and Chandon’s own notes call Pinot Noir the majority.

Guests ask whether this is the Moët they know. The honest answer: the same group founded Chandon, and Moët & Chandon’s Imperial Rosé is on our Bubbles rosé list.

Offer it to the guest who orders an Aperol spritz or an aperitivo: bittersweet orange under dry bubbles. Chandon suggests ice, an orange slice and rosemary; our glass and garnish come from the bar.

producer.who: Elio Perrone, a family wine estate
producer.where: Castiglione Tinella, province of Asti, Piedmont, Italy
producer.founded: The family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century
producer.history:
Elio Perrone is a family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti in Piedmont. Sources say the family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations. One profile dates the present generation’s taking over to 1989, when the son of the man whose name is on the label took the reins; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.

Moscato is the heart of the estate’s production. The family also farms vines at Isola d’Asti, where Barbera leads and Brachetto grows too, and the present generation created Bigaro, a blend of the two aromatic grapes made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.

Bigaro is its pink, softly sparkling wine: half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together and left a few days on the skins, with the fermentation stopped by filtering, so that it keeps some grape sugar and a light fizz at about 5 percent alcohol; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024. Brachetto brings red berries and rose, Moscato brings peach and orange blossom, and the colour is salmon. Its importer lists it as Piedmont DOC, and it is served well chilled, as an aperitif or with fruit desserts.

In the OBX it tops Gentilly Gin, peach and lemon, adding fruit, a soft sweetness and a gentle sparkle.
facts: A family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti, Piedmont.
The family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations, by the sources’ accounts.
One profile says the present generation took over in 1989; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.
The present generation created Bigaro, a Brachetto and Moscato blend made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.
Bigaro is half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together, left a few days on the skins, with fermentation stopped by filtering, leaving a light fizz and some sweetness.
About 5 percent alcohol on most listings; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024.
Brachetto brings red berries and rose; Moscato brings peach and orange blossom.
A salmon-coloured, softly sweet, gently sparkling wine, listed by its importer as Piedmont DOC.
notes: Say bee-gah-ROH. Call it a sparkling wine, never Champagne or Prosecco: it is a softly sweet, low-alcohol pink from Piedmont.
Guests ask why the OBX drinks so lightly. The honest answer: the Bigaro is about 5 percent alcohol, far below Champagne, though the gin still makes it a full cocktail.
Do not say what the name Bigaro means: an earlier note said mottled, but a fresh search could not confirm it.
Elio Perrone is the name on the label and the estate is family run. Name nobody else.
A guest who likes Moscato d’Asti will recognise the style: grapey, floral and gently sweet.

producer.founded: 1987 or 1988, as Sagpond Vineyards; later renamed Wölffer Estate Vineyard
producer.history:
Wölffer Estate began with Christian Wölffer, a German-born investor who bought farmland at Sagaponack, on Long Island, from 1978, first for a horse farm. The original vineyard, acquired in 1988, had been a potato field. The winery was founded as Sagpond Vineyards in 1987 or 1988, by different accounts, and later renamed Wölffer Estate Vineyard, in 1997 by one account, when a new winery opened. Its winemaker came from Germany in 1992 and is now a partner. Christian Wölffer died on New Year’s Eve 2008 in Brazil, and the estate is owned and run by his children with that partner. It is known above all for its rosé.

Wölffer began making non-alcoholic drinks in 1996, with verjus. In 2021 it launched Spring in a Bottle, a non-alcoholic sparkling rosé made in Germany from a certified organic vineyard in Rheinhessen, with the alcohol and other volatiles gently removed at a low 77°F. It also sells Petite Rosé, a sparkling drink pressed from unripe grapes, and a still Summer in a Bottle Rosé Zero.

A dealcoholised wine is made as wine first and then stripped of its alcohol: by vacuum distillation at low temperature, by a spinning cone column, which takes off the lightest aromas first and blends them back, or by reverse osmosis through fine membranes. Wölffer does not say which method it uses.

Guests ask whether it is truly zero. The honest answer: zero proof is not a legal term; listings give 0.0 percent and 0.5, so we read our label first.

producer.where: Sydney, Australia, by business databases; one account says it began in Britain
producer.history:
Lyre’s makes non-alcoholic spirits, drinks built to taste like gin, whisky, rum, agave spirit and the rest without the alcohol. The company dates itself to 2019 and says it was founded to replicate the world’s most popular spirits in a non-alcoholic form. It was started by two Australians; one account calls it a British company at the start, while business databases place its head office in Leichhardt, Sydney.

The name comes from the lyrebird, the Australian bird famous for mimicking birdsong and every other sound, even a mobile phone. A co-founder has said the range is meant to be the most successful mimic of classic spirits, and a lyrebird in a top hat sits on the neck of each bottle.

The Agave Blanco lists water, natural flavours, agave syrup, citric acid, salt, a stabiliser and a preservative; Lyre’s says its flavours and distillates come from seeds, botanicals, fruits and spices. Its American page calls it simply non-alcoholic, and an Australian listing gives under 0.5 percent alcohol. Under United States federal rules for malt beverages and dealcoholised wine, non-alcoholic means under 0.5 percent, while alcohol free means no alcohol at all.

The range runs to 13 spirits, sold in over 60 countries. In March 2025 Amber Beverage Group added Lyre’s to its portfolio; one report calls it a partnership and another an acquisition.

notes: Say LY-erz. Say non-alcoholic, never alcohol free or zero: Lyre’s labels it non-alcoholic, and an Australian listing gives under 0.5 percent.
The menu prints Lyre’s N/A Agave Tequila, but Lyre’s sells it as an agave spirit, not tequila. Say non-alcoholic agave.
Guests ask how it can taste like tequila. The honest answer: it is water built up with natural flavours, agave syrup and a little salt and acid, made to mimic one, as the lyrebird mimics.
Oh! What It Seemed to Be is the spirit-free twin of Old Buttermilk Sky, so a whole table can share the idea.
Pregnancy, medication or recovery questions go to the label and the bar; never promise zero.

producer.who: Abita Root Beer, Abita Brewing Company
producer.where: Abita Springs, Louisiana, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain
producer.founded: The root beer since the 1990s; the brewery 1986
producer.history:
Abita Root Beer is the soft drink of Abita Brewing, the brewery founded in 1986 in Abita Springs, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain, across the lake from New Orleans. The brewery’s own story is told with the Abita Amber of the Shells & Cheese; this profile keeps to the root beer, which was among the founding brewer’s recipes for the flagships.

Abita has brewed it since the 1990s; press material of 2015 and 2016 says for over 20 years. It is hot brewed rather than cold mixed, with spring water from Abita Springs, herbs, vanilla and yucca, which makes the foam, and it is sweetened only with Louisiana cane sugar, which the brewery likens to the soft drinks of the 1940s and 1950s, before bottlers turned to corn sugar. The brewery describes it as naturally caffeine free.

It went into cans in 2015, when the brewery reported making more than 14,000 barrels of it a year. Abita has also launched a hard root beer, Bayou Bootlegger; the menu prints Abita Root Beer, the soft drink.

At Brennan’s it is the fizz in Floating in South Africa, with Amarula Cream Liqueur and housemade vanilla bean ice cream.
facts: Made by Abita Brewing Company of Abita Springs, Louisiana, founded in 1986; the brewery’s own story is told with the Abita Amber.

Described by the brewery as naturally caffeine free.
Brewed since the 1990s; the founding brewer’s recipes for Abita’s flagships included the root beer.
In cans since 2015, when the brewery reported more than 14,000 barrels of root beer a year.
Abita’s hard root beer, Bayou Bootlegger, is a different product from the soft drink on our menu.

Guests ask whether the root beer has alcohol. Abita Root Beer is a soft drink; the alcohol in Floating in South Africa comes from the Amarula.

Questions about the ice cream or the cream go to the service note and the kitchen.
